speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 730. To provide for special expenditure in connection with a commission under the Inquiries Act to inquire into the working of the Patent Act, the Copyright Act, the Industrial Designs Act and other related legislation, $25,000.

maintopic: DEPRATMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this item asks for the expenditure of $25,000 to provide for the appointment of a commission under the Inquiries Act to inquire into the working

of the Patent Act, the Copyright Act, the Industrial Designs Act and other related legislation.
The Secretary of State told us on another occasion, in very general terms, of his intentions to appoint Mr. Justice Ilsley as commissioner. I think it would be of interest to hon. members if he were to expand upon what he said on the earlier occasion. It would be helpful if he would tell us in what respect the acts have been found to be inadequate, and the nature and scope of the inquiry which is proposed to be undertaken by the commissioner.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPRATMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I became Secretary of State there had been under consideration for some time a number of amendments to the Patent Act, one of which was actually introduced at the time I made the announcement in February with respect to the setting up of this commission.
It seemed to me, from such information as I was able to get on the subject-one which I admit, quite frankly, is new to me and with which I am not familiar-that some of these amendments were relatively far-reaching in their scope, and that there also appeared to be some need to consider some of the other procedures.
The matter had been under consideration for some time. After discussion with some of my colleagues, and such informal advice as I was able to get on the subject, it seemed to me it was sufficiently important to warrant an inquiry to find out what would really be the appropriate recasting of this patent legislation, which is very important from the point of view of the future industrial development of this country.
It was also represented to me by officials of the department that the Copyright Act was in considerable need, not merely of amendment but of complete overhaul; that it had not been revised for a good many years, and that many changes in the handling of copyright had developed in the interval. It was pointed out that the act really should be completely overhauled, as is customary in respect of all these pieces of legislation from time to time.
It was also drawn to my attention that the industrial designs act was really quite out of date, and that there had been tremendous development in industrial designs in recent years. Through the national gallery, with the assistance of the Department of Trade and Commerce, an attempt has been made to stimulate and promote industrial design in Canada, instead of relying, as we have in the past, upon work done in the United States, the United Kingdom and elsewhere.
Supply-Secretary of State
I have no doubt some hon. members have attended the exhibitions which have been held under the aegis of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in the old Laurentian club building in the last two years where, after competitions, the best designs have been selected. A lot of good work has been done here in the field of industrial design, and it is quite obvious that the legislation does need to be considered again, and that it is, in many respects which I will not attempt to enumerate because, quite frankly, I am not competent to do so, inadequate at the moment. That is precisely one of the reasons why it seems to me we should have some competent people to take a real look at these things. I do not think that most of us in the House of Commons would feel that we have sufficient detailed knowledge of these matters to consider new legislation without advice. It would be much better to have a report from really competent people who would hear interested parties and would be able to consider what the public interest really is.
Then, the Trade Marks Act was pretty thoroughly revised at the last session of the last parliament, and is to come into operation on July 1. It is not intended that this proposed commission of inquiry should give detailed consideration to that act. It would be prepared to hear recommendations, if the terms of reference we have in mind are adopted, and incidentally to give consideration to any representations which might be made as to improvements which might be made in that legislation as well. But there is no thought in that case of attempting to go over the whole of the generally excellent work done quite recently by parliament after a great deal of work by very competent people in the field. I do not think I can put in much briefer compass the kind of considerations the government had in mind than I did on February 11 last at page 1995 of Hansard where I said:
... it is the intention of the government within the next few months to establish a public inquiry-under the Inquiries Act into the working of the Patent Act, the Copyright Act, the industrial designs act and other related legislation.
Without attempting to give any specific terms of reference, I indicated that the general scope of the inquiry was to ensure:
. . . that adequate stimulus is being given to inventive and creative talent in Canada; to see that at the same time the public interest is being protected from undue exploitation of property in inventions and ideas.
It is my confident hope that a commission presided over by Chief Justice Ilsley will keep in mind these two considerations: The consideration that we do want to give adequate encouragement to invention and to

Supply-Secretary of State creativeness in Canada, and at the same time we do not want to create the kind of restrictions and monopolistic practices which will prevent the public from getting a proper benefit from such creativeness and inventiveness. That is about all that I can really usefully say at this stage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPRATMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this item presents the possibility of one of the most useful inquiries that could be held. Having regard to the fact that we have as yet no indication of the terms of reference, I feel it is appropriate to make certain comments on the assumption that the terms of reference have not yet been settled. Am I correct in that assumption?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPRATMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That assumption is quite correct. As a matter of fact it will be recalled, sir, that at the time I had that bill before the house I asked for comments, and the hon. member for Kamloops said there had not been any notice given of this and hon. members would naturally want to think about it. I thought that was a most reasonable view to take. And he said that surely the matter could wait until these estimates came up. I gave an undertaking at that time that the terms of reference would not be settled finally until an opportunity had been given for any hon. member who wished to do so to give his views, and that the government would take into consideration the views that were expressed in drawing up the reference. I can assure the Leader of the Opposition that no final decision has been made, and that the government will welcome any constructive suggestions from any quarter of the house in drawing up the terms of reference.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPRATMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was merely asking for information and not in any way challenging the position of the minister in presenting this item for the approval of the committee. I simply wished to be clear that even if there were a draft form of reference at the moment, I was directing remarks with the knowledge of that fact. I do therefore propose to make certain observations in regard to this subject, because the terms of reference under which this inquiry is conducted will, in a very large measure, indicate the pattern in respect of which the government is seeking information.
We have seen immense strides in this country within the past few years. One of the advantages of some accumulation of years is that it does make it possible to review within one's own memory the almost unbelievable changes that have taken place in this country in the past half century. From a country that was largely agricultural, and boasted of the fact that it was, we have


become a country that is predominantly industrial in the actual physical production, while at the same time recognizing that agriculture is still the basic industry of this country. This immense change has been based largely upon research, combined with the education received by young Canadians in our public and high schools and in our universities, particularly in the technical branches of those universities.
Within the years that have passed the names of many Canadians have become household words all over the world. That is not confined to industrial research. We all remember the name of Saunders and his effect on agricultural production. We all remember the name of Banting, and millions of people over the world remember it from day to day with a tremendous sense of personal indebtedness. We all know the name of Best and his magnificent contribution to the preservation of blood plasma as well as his participation in the development of insulin. Within recent years we also have seen some remarkable developments in the province of Quebec, under the council that has been established there to encourage new types of ceramic and metal production. There are a number of names that I could mention now that are becoming well known far outside of Canada as a result of that planned activity. I could go on and mention many others in the aircraft industry and in other types of industry whose inventions and names are well known.
Having said all that, I think it is important for us to realize that a great part of our expansion has been the direct result of the impact on our lives of the demands of other nations through two world wars. God forbid that anyone should suggest that wars in themselves have been beneficial in their effect. Certainly that is not my suggestion. Nevertheless, this is the process of history. Other countries have had the same experience in other times. Nations which had exhausted their basic resources, that had a highly-developed skill accumulated throughout long years, found it necessary to look to other lands for those raw materials. In that process those other lands have advanced and in turn have learned how to use the raw material.
In the first world war we suddenly found that we could produce new types of heavy equipment. Our production of guns, of munitions of war and of many of the medical supplies opened new fields of industrial development in this country which after the war were turned to the advantage of our people in employment and in prosperity. Having learned something of our resources through necessity, other countries then turned more

and more to Canada after world war I. They not only looked upon us as the source of raw materials but they also brought their industrial plants here and started production here because of cheap power, because of the availability of resources, and because of the fact that we have very satisfactory water routes through which to carry our production to the markets of the world. In addition to that was the fact that being as close as we are to the coal producing areas of the United States we were able to find the industrial fuel in the central parts of the country as well as in the maritimes and in Alberta. Perhaps there may be some measure of regret in connection with that in the maritimes and in Alberta because undoubtedly it is limiting the employment of coal in the central part of Canada because of the greater availability of anthracite and bituminous coal from the mines of the United States which are fairly close to us.
Simply mentioning that indicates the kind of challenge that is presented to us. I am convinced that one of the ways in which to use our great coal resources in this country, and we sometimes forget that today we have the largest known undeveloped coal resources in the world, is to find new processes by which coal can be used for other things than fuel, and also for use as fuel in a liquid form as has been done in other countries.
I recall on different occasions seeing exhibitions in Germany and Czechoslovakia of the really fantastic products made from coal. I recall one exhibit at the world fair in Paris in 1937 which was wholly devoted to products produced from coal. I recall that you could get everything from your hat to your shoes made from coal, and I might add that this was a German exhibit.
Far from those things being ersatz products in the term of contempt in which that word- was sometimes used, those products were enduring and had the quality particularly of holding dyes and things of that kind which made many of them more enduring in some cases than other products made with more conventional material. We even found sweetening material being used instead of sugar and that material came from coal.
All these things are merely a hint of the possibilities that exist in the development of our coal resources by applied research. It may be well for us to recall that at the time Britain was regularly winning the Schneider trophy before the war with the fastest piston engine airplanes, the engines were powered by liquid fuel made from coal.
There is a challenge to us to seek new methods of employment of the vast resources of coal in the maritimes and in Alberta, and
Supply-Secretary of State may I, by way of comment, simply mention the fact that in a number of places in Europe they are developing electric energy from the burning of coal in seams underground, and producing electric energy at costs a little higher than hydroelectric power. That is being carried on today with tremendous success in Russia, Germany, and in Poland. So much for that particular field of research. That is merely a hint, I think, of the wide scope for research of this kind.
But I come back to the fact that in this great development that has taken place in the years during and since the last war we have been very largely the heirs or assigns, or perhaps I should put it the other way and say the assigns or heirs to inventions in the United States, Great Britain, Germany, and other countries. We have been the assigns in the case of the United States and Britain, and we have been the heirs through a process of international legal procedure in the case of Germany, Japan, and some other countries.
Our automobile production, our electrical production, our employment of wood resources, most of these things largely employ at this time the patents and design that have been the result of long years of research and experiment in the United States. But that is only natural. Companies like the Ford Motor Company, General Motors, and Chrysler very naturally make automobiles of the same design and pattern as those which have come off the drafting boards in the United States as a result of research there. In the case of great electrical companies like General Electric, Westinghouse and English Electric, there again we use very largely the patents, designs and research of the parent organizations in the United States and Britain of those companies which have been located in Canada.
There has, of course, been very considerable Canadian development in the field of research. I suggest, however, that here is one field in which Canadians today are challenged to establish their own independence and to follow a new line in industry, in the employment of agricultural production, in the employment of many of our new-found minerals, in the employment of various products used, particularly those used in the employment of our seafood and fresh water food, along different lines than have yet been discovered in any other land. After all, no 15 million people in the world today have the bounty which Providence has placed at our disposal, and the value of that bounty will in large measure be determined by research which will decide the kind of final product that goes to the consumer from these various things.

Supply-Secretary of State
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do speak on this subject in some detail because it happens to be a subject with which I was closely associated not so many years ago. As the minister knows, research in this country is carried on not only in the government field by the national research council, but also by the Ontario research foundation, the research council of Alberta, the British Columbia research council, the research foundation of Nova Scotia, and the specialized research organizations in the province of Quebec where they have been set up in different specialized fields. These organizations have done great work but one of the things I found in my earlier inquiry into this subject at the time I had the responsibility for introducing certain legislation in the Ontario legislature was that there is a great need for information about research, for the pooling of research knowledge, and for the integration of research generally by voluntary efforts based upon readily available information.
Merely to give an example of the almost incredible duplication we found in some cases, I discovered on inquiry that at the time we were setting up a new research group to co-ordinate research there were three different organizations which, unknown to each other, were conducting research into blood diseases then affecting partridge in the province of Ontario. It was fairly extensive research. Of course, it was something that affected the tourist business and the people that were interested in sport. For instance, people making ammunition were interested in there being more partridge; sportsmen were interested in there being more partridge; and the government was interested in the disease which possibly might be contagious and might affect other birds or even animals. As the result of the setting up of this integrating committee, that inquiry was all co-ordinated into one single research activity.
We found other cases of duplication and multiplication in matters that to some might seem to be more important than were the mortal statistics of the partridge population of the province of Ontario. However, this procedure was welcomed. I know that the same experience has been found by the national research council as that found by these other provincial organizations I have mentioned. Mr. Chairman, it is a fact, however, that a great deal of patient and constant educational work needs to be done in this country in order to demonstrate to our manufacturers that co-operation in research is not in conflict with normal healthy competition in most cases but that, in fact, it is to the mutual advantage of all.

What is known as group research-and that is a name that now has special significance-is developing rather slowly in Canada. We have one example of group research in Canada that is a stimulating example of what can be done. It is in the Sarnia field where both the public development in the Polymer plant and the private development in the Dow Chemical plant are associated in an effective partnership along with other new industries that have recently started there and are carrying on very successfully different types of group research.
Canada today is operating in a highly competitive market. We have said that before. We should continue to repeat it. What we face is not merely a competition based upon the skill of the worker, the energy and drive of management or the availability of capital. It is something that is based upon the research which will put in the hands of the ultimate consumer the highest quality product that can come from any particular article. Why is it that today most people concede that Germany produces the best camera equipment? We had some reference to a German company which has recently set up in Canada and which is developing here a new and highly successful industry based upon German research. It is because of their tremendous concentration on research. A large part of the almost unbelievable revival of industrial production in western Germany is the result of the devotion of an extremely large part of their manpower to pure research. As a result, in Germany today there will be seen in the shops articles not only of high quality but of new design and of new uses which are giving many of the producers an advantage in world competition in these days.
I should like to say that, along with group research, we have evidence of what can be achieved by highly specialized research. One of the most remarkable examples in the world-if not perhaps the most remarkable one-of the value of pure research is to be found at the Philips electric plant at Eindhoven in Holland. There, in a country that could be contained within the boundaries of lake Ontario, where a population much smaller than ours occupies that small land area, there is to be found an industrial plant employing more than 30,000 workmen in one place as well as with subsidiary plants in other places. Their world position in the highly competitive field of electrical production, and particularly electronics, has been based on the concentration on pure research.
In Eindhoven alone I found over 2,000 men and women working on nothing but pure

research. As a result, they have been years ahead in many new types of production in the electronic and mechanical-electric field and in the heavy electrical production field. It is that factor alone, along with the skill of the workmen, the drive of the management and the availability of markets by seaborne routes, that has given them this tremendous industry in what is such a comparatively small country.
I mention this example to suggest the wide, almost limitless field for inquiry that exists. In this country with our enormous resources, how can we put those raw materials to still greater effect than is now being done in Holland where they must import all their raw materials and yet are able to produce this extraordinary result because of research itself? How can we widen in every way the employment of our agricultural products, of which we have such an abundance? Agricultural chemurgy is today one specialized field of chemical research that needs to be explored in this country in order to find new ways of turning into finished industrial products the enormous food surpluses we normally have. In our competition not only with the United States and Britain but with Germany and Japan as well,-and I would underline Germany and Japan with their high skill and low wages-we must in this competitive world be prepared to meet them on even terms. We can only do that by a process of education and encouragement of research, along with inquiry into practical methods of research.
While I certainly believe in the encouragement of such examples of private research as are to be found in the Philips plant in Eindhoven-yes, are to be found in some of our great wood products industries in this country today-may I suggest that we should also remember that there may be some types of development where, under the national research council or some of the provincial research organizations, pilot plants may well be the answer to the problem. Those pilot plants might be conducted in co-operation with industry or separately, all depending on the particular circumstances. This also is a field of exploration that is before us.
All I have sought to do, Mr. Chairman, is by illustration to express my own belief in the vital importance of research to Canada at this time and to suggest some lines of inquiry which this commission might follow in seeking to place before the government recommendations or legislation that would encourage research throughout Canada.
I want to go back and to say only a few words about one subject I mentioned before.
Supply-Secretary of State I mentioned what happened in the case of the invention of the jet engine by a young Englishman named Whittle. I recalled that Sir Robert Watson-Watt, the man primarily responsible for the invention of that other great development of the war period, radar, had pointed out that as the result of a certain lack of supervision of patents and through no fault of Whittle, certainly through no lack of loyalty or intense devotion to the British cause, the patent of this new device had become public property. I pointed out that German agents had obtained full drawings of the patent and that actually, although it was a British invention, the Germans had produced jet engines before they were produced in Britain with the result that many of the jets that have been employed by the Russians in the past few years are the direct heirs and descendants of that unfortunate accident.
I say that because we all know that Russian jet development is almost entirely dependent upon the fact that Russia occupied East Germany where the great engine plants had been established to keep them as far away as possible from British, American and Canadian bombing, and that therefore they acquired these plants where they still stood and they absorbed much of the technical skill that was available. I want to repeat that this was not something merely to illustrate caution. That was a tragic incident that has actually increased the danger to the whole world on a scale that we can hardly yet realize. It is likely that those who saw that huge Tupelov bomber fly over Red square a few weeks ago would not have seen such an event for years to come had it not been for the accidental discovery of that patent through the very simple circumstance that it was patented in the ordinary way and became available to German agents who passed it on to their own government.
Along with the inquiry into ways by which we can encourage research, may I most strongly urge that an inquiry also be conducted into the way in which, without in any way limiting the initiative of our people and suppressing inventive development, we may seek to avoid a repetition of that tragic event which has greatly increased the danger to every one of us at this time.
This is a subject perhaps second to none in its importance to the development of Canada. Research at a high level, research such as is applied to industry in Germany, Japan, Holland, the United States and Britain at this time, can expand employment enormously in the use of the resources we possess. This inquiry could well open the door to new

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DEPRATMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I have listened carefully, as I think every other hon. member did, to the most interesting and, for me, in many respects instructive observations made by the Leader of the Opposition. Of course I know that he understands as well as the rest of us that the only way in which this commission of inquiry can promote research is an indirect one. The positive promotion by the federal authorities of research is the responsibility of such organisms as the national research council, the defence research board, the fisheries research council, the various research organizations in the Department of Agriculture, the bureau of mines and a great many other places in the federal government, as well as of provincial agencies and university bodies to which the hon. gentleman referred.
I do think, however, that his contribution was in no sense irrelevant because I think it is most important that the patent law and the law with respect to industrial design should be considered precisely from the points of view the hon. member mentioned. In other words, the primary purpose of having


patents, as I conceive it, is not to create or consecrate a particular kind of private property for the benefit of some individual to be used selfishly for his own good; it is primarily to give stimulus to inventiveness because it is believed that such stimulus is in the public interest. To the extent to which our law can be so drafted and administered that it does tend to encourage Canadians to do independent research and encourages them by giving them the benefit of their research, to that extent will the industrial and other developments which are based on that kind of research also benefit.
I do feel, and it is one of the reasons the government felt it was desirable to have a commission of inquiry, that the first and most important consideration in the minds of the commissioners should be how will these laws conduce to the development of this country. I think that the Leader of the Opposition, by emphasizing the points he did-and I shall see that they are drawn to the attention of the commission of inquiry-will give an orientation to the inquiry which will be most helpful.
With respect to the question of maintaining proper security for patents that are of significance from the point of view of the defence of the country, I indicated the other day on the third reading of the bill that was before the house at that time, and I do not think I can indicate any more than that, that the present law does contain about as much protection as anybody has been able to conceive it is possible to put in the law itself. But I will certainly suggest to the commissioners that they should give consideration to any method by which they think the law can be strengthened.
I think the Leader of the Opposition is right in feeling that it is not so much the words of the law as the way that it is administered and the vigilance with which these things are scrutinized to make sure, when an application is made to patent any invention such as the one to which he referred, that before publicity of any kind is given to it it is referred to the proper organization, such as the defence research board, which body can consider its merits and exercise their best judgment as to whether or not it is the kind of thing which requires secrecy for national security reasons.
As to the question of procedure, I have had one or two discussions with Chief Justice Ilsley about the way in which the inquiry will be carried on. I do not think it would be wise to commit the commission in advance by saying that they would not sit anywhere except in Ottawa. Personally I hope it will not be necessary to go anywhere else. I do

not feel that this is the kind of inquiry where, in the normal course, it should be necessary to travel about the country. I conceive that the number of people who will wish to make representations will be relatively small, as it is a relatively specialized field. It would probably be quite adequate to provide for hearings here in Ottawa. I do not think it would be wise to limit the commission.
It is not intended that Chief Justice Ilsley should be the sole commissioner. Perhaps I might disclose to the committee that the government has already given consideration to the personnel of the commission and it is intended to ask, in addition to Chief Justice Ilsley, Mr. Guy Favreau, who is a member of the restrictive trade practices commission and Mr. W. W. Buchanan, who is a member of the tariff board, to be commissioners with Chief Justice Ilsley. The reason for the selection of these two gentlemen is that there is an obvious relationship between the fields of patents and copyright on the one hand, and restrictive practices, as well as the administration of customs on the other. It was felt that it would be of benefit to the inquiry to have the particular kind of experience these gentlemen already have in the ordinary occupations in which they are serving, and that their service on this commission would increase their value as public servants when they have completed this work.
Now, as to technical assistance Chief Justice Ilsley is giving some consideration to the kind and extent of technical assistance he will need, apart from such assistance as will be provided by the government through its regular agencies, such as the commissioner of patents-

I plan to have some discussions myself with the chief justice, and the officers of my department will be having them as well. Our feeling is that the commission itself will have to decide what it needs, and what it needs it will get.
Perhaps I should say one more word about the amount. This is a real estimate. It is perhaps a "guesstimate", if I may use the language of Time magazine. No one can forecast very accurately, except in relation to previous experience what such a commission will cost.

I am sure that will have been carefully considered, but it is a caution which occurs to me. We are all extremely interested in the protection of the small businessman who

It was felt that priority would have to be given to the primary duties of Mr. Favreau as a member of the restrictive trade practices commission, but that his services were so desirable on other grounds that this inquiry would adapt itself to the exigencies of the other service.
It is not my expectation that it will be possible for this commission to complete its work in time to contemplate any legislation at the next session of parliament. On this item, Mr. Chairman, I think it is appropriate to raise several matters of a general nature. The one which I have particularly in mind to discuss is the matter of the security screening system in practice for the purpose of ensuring that all those in the public service shall be loyal to Canada and to no other country. There has been considerable discussion of this matter during this session, largely by way of question and answer and also considerable comment on it in the press.
Before I proceed with any general remarks, I should like to ask the minister if he will indicate whether, as a result of any consideration the government may have given following that earlier discussion, there are any substantial changes in the method now

being followed or in the government's readiness to give information which previously has been withheld. This might obviate the necessity for any remarks at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The answer to my hon.
friend's question is no.

Then, I should like to proceed by reviewing in as brief a fashion as I can the discussions that have taken place in the past, and laying before the committee some reasons that I believe indicate there should be a substantial change in the policy of the government, not only with respect to its machinery for carrying out any screening but with respect to its policy of giving information to this country on the results of those efforts.
I state at the outset my opinion that there is an entirely undesirable and unnecessary degree of secrecy surrounding this matter of security within the public service. There can be surely no disagreement on the general principle that, in the light of the revelations made here in 1945 and 1946, and more recently in Australia in connection with the Petrov case, and what we know generally of communist methods, it is essential that industry, government, and all those concerned with the particular or general administration of our affairs should ensure to the maximum possible degree that those who are charged with responsibility in any way in connection with the handling of those affairs should be loyal to Canada, and should not have communist loyalty.
It is on that basis that the security program was set up. I feel also that there would be no disagreement with two other general provisions of the program, the first of which is the desirability of ensuring that the program is as effective as it can be made to accomplish its object of screening out all those as to whose loyalty there is reason for question or doubt. And, along with that, there should be the fulfilment of the desire to ensure that the working of that system is not unfair to those who may come under suspicion. It is in connection with the problem of compromising those two equally desirable objectives, the efficiency of the screening system and its effectiveness, and the preservation of fairness to those who may be subject to review, that the difficulty seems to lie.
I suggest that what has been revealed during the past session, and on earlier occasions, indicates that our system falls down badly under both these headings. The reasons I advance in support of that proposition are those features which have emerged from the discussion of the subject. The first is the unreasonable and, I think, the dangerous

refusal of this government to give information as to what results have been achieved by security measures. I wish to be careful not to make any statements which are not based on facts. But here we are left to draw our own conclusions in the realm of fancy, and that is as a result of the government's refusal to give information to which I submit the house and the country are properly entitled.
It is difficult therefore to make statements on the basis of fact. Nevertheless I think we do have to draw such conclusions as it is reasonable to draw from the situation as we find it. And it is as consistent with the government's refusal to give information to draw the conclusion that the results of their system have not been effective as it would be to draw the conclusion that they have been effective. If they have been effective, then I can see no reason why the results should not be made known. Because I submit those results can be made known in a manner which is not unfair to any individual, and which would result in no prejudice either to the private or public interest.
What is the history of this refusal to give information? The government says it cannot be given without prejudice to individuals. Well, so far as this year is concerned, on March 3 I began to ask detailed questions regarding the government's security screening program. It was on that date that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as the Acting Prime Minister, refused that information. The following question, to which an answer was refused, is found at page 2618 of Hansard:
1.	Since January 1, 1947, how many dominion government employees of all categories have been screened out of their former positions for security reasons in each department, agency, or crown corporation?
2.	Of these (a) how many have been dismissed from the department, agency or crown corporation in question; (b) how many have been moved to other less sensitive positions?
No name was asked for; not even the identification of a position within a department was asked for. All that was asked was a simple total, broken down by departments, agencies of government or crown corporations. On that occasion the Acting Prime Minister said:
In my opinion it is not in the public interest to say why people were dismissed from the service, whether it was on security grounds or otherwise.
I submit it is very much in the public interest to know whether people have been dismissed from the public service on security grounds. It is in the public interest, and for two reasons: First, we are entitled to know whether disloyal people have been found in the public service and, if so, what damage may have been done during the period they were in it. Secondly, we are entitled to know
Supply-Justice
how effective government measures are, by which they are seeking to protect the public interest and the loyalty of our public service. How can it be argued that this parliament, which represents the people of Canada, is not entitled to information of that kind, and is not entitled to know whether people have been dismissed from the service on security grounds?
I pointed out to the Acting Prime Minister on that date that the questions as asked would not give the identity of any individual. I am prepared to admit that unless an individual himself seeks to make a public issue of it, and is prepared to have it made public, he is entitled to such protection as he can be given in connection with these security matters. I pointed out to the Acting Prime Minister- the Minister of Trade and Commerce-on that occasion that no individual would be identified by giving an answer to the questions in the form in which they were asked. I pressed him for a reconsideration of his decision. That reconsideration was refused, and the questions were ordered to be dropped.
In the course of that further discussion the Minister of Trade and Commerce used a word, the use of which I cannot believe was other than deliberate, because the question had been under consideration and had appeared on the order paper for some days. He used the word "McCarthyism" in a context which could only have the implication that those who sought to obtain any information whatsoever about this matter were guilty of that particular form of activity. In what I shall have to say a little later I think it will emerge clearly that if there is any "McCarthyism" involved here it rests squarely with the government, and the likelihood of it is made more probable because of the course of action followed by the government itself in connection with its whole program of security screening.
Here, this type of factual information as to the totals of those affected is denied. We do not find that to be the situation in the United States or in Great Britain. I am not referring at all to the particular committee in the United States headed by the senator whose name is so well known to us here. But there are other and more appropriate methods of inquiry being conducted down there by the executive itself, following procedures which I think it might be generally agreed are on a sound and proper basis.
By coincidence, on the very same day that the answers were being refused to the Canadian people, similar information was being made available by the executive of the United States to the people of the United States. I have a report which appeared in the New

Supply-Justice
York Times of March 3. Actually it was given down there the previous day. It was given in Washington on March 2. Here are some examples of the information which the people of the United States are given as to the effectiveness of their security screening program. The article commences:
383 persons were included today in a broadly-defined subversive category among 2,427 security risk separations from government employment during the final seven months of 1953. Philip Young, chairman of the civil service commission, explained to a Senate committee however, that he could not say any or all of the 383 were either communists or subversives.
He said they had "derogatory material of a substantial nature in their personnel file".
Therefore, without identifying anybody the total is given. A little later in the article it indicates that a complete breakdown of the results of their security screening program has also been given. It reported a total of 1,074 dismissals and 1,353 resignations under the security program between May 28 and December 31 last year. Mr. Young gave this breakdown, and the article continues to give other figures. It is a very complete breakdown of a total of over 2,000 cases. That is the type of information that I asked for here in this house on March 3 and was refused by the Canadian government on that day, but which had been given to the United States people just one day before.
Then, in case it is felt that the practice in the United States is coloured by what goes on there under the guise of McCarthyism- although I point out that this was not a McCarthy type of inquiry, this was a careful, cautious, and sensible statement made by the executive, in contrast to the other-but in case it is felt that what is done down there under the present circumstances would not be a safe example, I refer to the practice in Great Britain, where on at least two occasions to my knowledge and I should think probably far more, very complete information has been given as to the results of the government security screening program, as to what has been found, the number of dismissals, and so on. In 1950 information was given out through the British information service as follows:
The number of cases considered by the end of April, 1S50 was 86, of which one was because of membership in the fascist party. The following table shows the disposition of the cases considered.
Then, they give a breakdown as to how that whole 86 are made up. It might be interesting to read this into the record:
Transferred to non-secret departments .... 32
Resigned	 5
Exonerated and reinstated	 19
That, Mr, Chairman, is a most interesting figure, in view of what I shall have to say 
under the second general heading of my criticism of the government's security methods; that is, that they do not come up to standard on the point of preserving fairness to the dismissed civil servant because there is no appeal system provided here as there is in the United Kingdom. It is very interesting to note that under their system 19 suspected civil servants were exonerated and
reinstated. The breakdown continues:
Dismissed, (including 1	fascist)	 7
Retired for health reasons before completion
of investigations	  1
On special leave, either sub judice or confirmed communists awaiting transfer or dismissal	 2
I can see no reason why that sort of information should not be given here. Indeed, there is no reason, there can be no justification, for refusal of similar information in Canada. That was April, 1950. On a later occasion similar information was given in the British House of Commons. Actually, this information came to my attention through a United States newspaper, the Christian Science Monitor, of March 17, 1954, which contained a report reading as follows:
British security investigations have resulted in the dismissal of 24 British civil servants, chancellor of the exchequer Richard Butler told the House of Commons. Another 72 persons have been transferred to other duties, he said.
It will be seen, Mr. Chairman, that that statement of 1954 brings more up to date the statement given up to the end of April, 1950.
I have not taken the time to make a detailed check of the British Hansard to find if there were other occasions when these periodic reports on the results and the effectiveness of their security system were made to their house, but I should think it is probably extremely likely. And since what has been said makes perfectly evident that the United Kingdom, which pays as much attention to the question of the security and the dignity of the individual as we do here, finds this factual information as to the total number affected can be given without prejudice to them at all, then there is no justifiable reason whatsoever why the same course should not be followed here.
I have indicated that on March 3 an attempt to get this sort of information was refused by the government. I have indicated that in other jurisdictions that information is given. In case it might be felt that that was an isolated case and that the government would perhaps reconsider it, I made another effort to obtain factual information. The question appeared in Hansard of March 25, 1954 and was answered on March 29. The question was as follows:
On the occasion when the loyalty screening of government employees was first completed, were

there any dismissals or transfers, and if so, how many, in the following departments or agencies of government; (a) external affairs; (b) national defence; (e) national research council; (d) Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (both domestic and international services); (e) national film board?
I think it will be agreed, Mr. Chairman, that generally speaking these are very important departments or agencies of government having to deal, as they do, with matters vital to our national defence, or alternatively matters of general informational services where communist leanings or communist loyalties could be most disastrous from the point of view of their effect on the material which goes out over those services. Therefore it is a very important thing for the people of Canada to know how effective has been the result of the government screening in these vital departments. The answer was given by the Prime Minister himself on this occasion as follows:
The only answer I can make is that this government must take the responsibility of refusing to make a public record of the information requested by the question for the reasons given by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) in answering orally a similar question on March 3.
So that the decision of the government remains the same. This information, of a type which is available to the people of the United States and of the United Kingdom, is not to be made available to the Canadian people through their House of Commons. I pointed out immediately to the Prime Minister, Mr. Chairman, as you will probably recall, that similar information had been given here on a previous occasion with respect to the national film board. On that occasion, when we asked a question as to how many releases for security reasons had been made from that board we were given the figures. They will be found at page 1343 of Hansard of March 29, 1950 when, after having made a general report on the screening of the national film board, the minister was asked a question as to the numbers released, and he replied as follows:
Perhaps I should tell the house that during the course of the screening there were some 580 odd files examined, and as a result thereof, and for reasons which could be attributed to the security screening, there were three separations from the board.
I also find that on another occasion in 1950 I asked a question as to the number of separations from the national research council for security reasons and I was given the information that two had been thus separated. On that occasion we were given their actual positions on the board. Therefore, back in 1950 there was no objection to answering one or two isolated questions and answering them in more detail than they are now being asked. Yet, in 1954 questions dealing with
Supply-Justice
exactly similar matters in a more general form with less detail are being refused. In 1950 the government was willing to say how many separations had been made from the national film board for security reasons, and in 1954 it is not.
What reason, Mr. Chairman, can there be? What harm was done by information given in 1950, except perhaps to the government? What harm was done to the general interest or welfare which could result in a change of decision? I suggest that we can only draw the conclusion with which we are left, and on the basis of lack of information that conclusion is as logical as any other conclusion can be, namely that the only interest which could suffer is that of the government, and that it is for that reason they do not wish to disclose this information. That is the reason for the change of heart and the change of attitude between 1950 and 1954.
Whatever the reason I submit that the present policy is wrong and unjustified, and indeed is dangerous rather than beneficial to the public interest, because I submit it is dangerous to leave the people of Canada in the dark as to the effectiveness of the government's security screening measures.
Not only are we refused information as to the effectiveness of these measures from the point of view of the number of dismissals which may have resulted, and which would enable us to make some estimate as to whether this screening is being vigorously and successfully pursued, but we are also denied information as to who is carrying it out. The Canadian people are not to be permitted to know the personnel who are in large measure charged with supplying the advice on which a decision is made as to whether a civil servant should be removed. I can think of nothing more important for us to know, and no information to which we are more entitled, than the names of the persons who are in charge of this highly important and in fact vital duty in connection with the protection of the public interest.
But hon. members will recall that when we asked the names of the personnel of the security panel, the security panel which, as I understand it, passes on the more important cases of security investigations, we were told that it is an established and general principle to preserve the anonymity of civil servants serving on interdepartmental committees of this nature. All we are to know is that this panel is made up of senior officers of government departments which are themselves most concerned with security matters. We were not even to know whether the present Secretary of State on a former occasion served on the secretariat of

Supply-Justice
that panel. He was not being asked whether he is a member of the panel now. We asked whether he had formerly been on it. Perhaps the mistake I made was asking whether, if he had been on it, he has now an opportunity to answer officially any questions with relation to the work of the panel, because I can imagine the government saying, "Oh, oh, if we say he was on it then perhaps he will be pressed to give an answer to some questions so we had better hide again behind this cloak of secrecy and simply say we are not going to say whether he was on it or not." Of course, it is a matter of general knowledge that the present Secretary of State was on the secretariat at the time when he-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That it not correct.

Well, now we have the answer to my question, Mr. Chairman, and how much and simpler it would have been if the government had said "No" when I asked the question some two or three months ago. Now we have got that information-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We thought he was ubiquitous.

-and it need not have been necessary to take so long to get it. The Secretary of State now indicates he is willing to give some answers to these questions: I hope his attitude will permeate the epidermis of the Minister of Justice and produce in him some reaction and also in the Prime Minister, so that we can perhaps have a realistic approach to this question of security screening and find out some information as to what is going on and who is carrying out this work. Perhaps I may ask the Secretary of State while he is in this answering mood, if he will tell us whether he is on the security panel at the present time?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He is as silent as the Minister of agriculture was a little while ago.

We will leave him to think that one over. The second branch on which I suggest our security screening system falls far short of the desirable standard is that it does not ensure that there will be the maximum possible fairness to the individual who may come under security investigation.
But perhaps, Mr. Chairman, before I go on to that I might mention one other factor in connection with the important point that this house is entitled to information as to who is carrying out this work, and is entitled to know who is serving on the security panel. One of the reasons why we seek this information is that we cannot but help recall with considerable misgiving, when we think about it, the examples of inefficiency

in the past with respect to this matter of security in the public service. We think of revelations at the time of the royal commission on espionage when it was made clear to what extent there had been communist infiltration into the public service. That started the matter off. We have to remember that there had been that infiltration and no one in the government knew anything about it.
Then we were further disturbed to learn that, notwithstanding that there had been a notebook turned over by Mr. Gouzenko, showing among others the name of Klaus Fuchs, that matter had not been followed up with the result that Fuchs continued for an appreciable period to turn over to his Russian masters secrets of vital importance to the defence of the free world. Although this name had been in the notebook turned over by Mr. Gouzenko, when I pressed in 1950 for information regarding measures taken to investigate the names of others in the notebook we got answers which are masterpieces as an example of lack of information. They were lengthy, courteous, but completely uninformative as to what was being done to follow up and to make sure that all those with their names in the notebook had been investigated, and that those who could genuinely be suspected with regard to their loyalty had been removed from the public service.
We could obtain no information to satisfy us that the government had acted vigorously under that heading. And I was disturbed to find out just recently, from an answer given to me by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, that although Sam Carr was clearly shown to be involved in this espionage ring and was also shown to have obtained his certificate of naturalization by fraud, that that certificate has not been revoked.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would my hon. friend state the nature of the fraud?

It will be found in the report of the royal commission on espionage that at the time when he made his application for citizenship he said in evidence that he had no loyalty to any country other than Canada, and it was later found that at the very time he made that statement he was engaged in espionage. If the minister cares to read the report of the royal commission with particular reference to Sam Carr he will find very interesting reading showing the extent to which efforts were made to give Carr his citizenship at the very time when he was engaged in espionage.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I read the report.

That man is now free to wander about the world with a valid certificate of naturalization giving him all the position- until it is revoked-of a Canadian citizen. But in the answer given to me by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration it is stated clearly that Sam Carr swore an oath or subscribed to a declaration of allegiance. I had better read the question and the answer. The question is as follows:
In order to obtain his certificate of naturalization on March 1, 1945, did Sam Carr swear an oath or subscribe to a declaration of allegiance or make any other form of affirmation of loyalty to His Majesty and to Canada?
The answer is: yes. Well, on March 1, 1945, he was up to his neck in espionage under orders from his Russian masters, yet swearing allegiance to Canada and to His Majesty. The second question was as follows:
Has his grant of naturalization ever been revoked on grounds that it was obtained by false representations or on any other grounds?
The answer is: no. The result is, as I have said, that Sam Carr is now free to produce that certificate which has the effect of enabling him to say "I am a Canadian citizen"-and it has never been revoked- wherever he may go.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I turn to the second ground of criticism of the government's security screening measures, namely, that they have in them all the elements which make them potentially unfair and in fact unfair to civil servants who may be investigated. I would point out that under the Canadian system there exists no right of appeal by any civil servant who may be suspected or who may have been dismissed from his position or transferred to a less sensitive position on security grounds. That fact was made clear in lengthy answers to questions asked in the house and which I need not summarize in detail because I am sure the effect of them will be fresh in the minds of the members of the committee.
It will be recalled that the explanation was given that in arriving at their decisions as to the suitability of a civil servant to continue in his present employment, there were taken into account the associations of that civil servant with others who may be suspected or be known to be disloyal. The explanation was also given that when a decision v/as being arrived at as to the suitability or otherwise of the civil servant to continue in his employment, he was not confronted, as a general rule, with the statement that he was suspected and was not given an opportunity to clear himself of the suspicion. We therefore have two features. First, we have what can only be called the principle of guilt by association accepted in this method.
Supply-Justice
Second, we have the fact that the man suspected and in effect found guilty and removed from his employment is not given an opportunity to meet the case against him.
When you realize, Mr. Chairman, that those two aspects are present under our screening system, and then remember that the Minister of Trade and Commerce used the word "McCarthyism" as applied to those who were trying to get information on these things on March 3, 1954, I think you will agree with me when I say that, if there is McCarthyism here, you can see where it lies.
There are other and older forms than that one of vile investigating methods-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. When the committee rose at one o'clock some of the heat which we expect to find soon outside the chamber had apparently made itself apparent inside the chamber. The Minister of Justice had been addressing himself to a question of privilege and the Leader of the Opposition had risen on a point of order. During the luncheon adjournment, I had the opportunity of perusing Hansard, and after such perusal I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to citations 191, 192 and 193 of Beauchesne, third edition. I shall only refer to them briefly. Citation 191 reads in part as follows.
Only in very aggravated cases, requiring the immediate interposition of the house, will any business be suddenly interrupted.
In citation 192 we find the following:
A dispute arising between two hon. members as to allegations of facts hardly fulfils the conditions of a privileged question, and, if deemed to be a matter to be at once entertained, it is more convenient to postpone other business rather than extend the area of privilege.
I am of the opinion that perhaps there is not a true question of privilege here and that the hon. member for Kamloops should be allowed to continue. May I point out that under ordinary circumstances the time of the hon. member for Kamloops would have expired at one o'clock, but, owing to the interruption while we were discussing the question of privilege and the point of order, I think he is entitled to at least an additional five minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for the care with which you have considered these matters. I should like to suggest that if you had gone on to citation 193 you might read into the record a reference to "so-called questions of privilege" which I would think would be the category in which this one would fall.
The subject I was dealing with when the minister raised his point was that the procedure the government follows in dealing with these matters of security is such as to open the door to the possibility of unfairness and, indeed, I submit there is inherent in the whole procedure itself an element of unfairness in that a decision will be arrived at in part upon the basis of the associations of the civil servant under suspicion to which that civil servant has no opportunity to answer. It is not only because of the possibility of an adverse decision being arrived at on the basis of association but on the general principle that a man who is suspected is apt to suffer prejudice to himself as a result of the suspicions against him and should have the opportunity to know the case and to answer it. That is inherent in our whole system of justice, and while I do not overlook the point that has been made before that here men are not, in the strict sense, on trial, nevertheless I submit the same principles apply.
There can be no more fundamental right than the right to a livelihood, the right to work, and yet that right is placed in jeopardy and the person apt to lose it has no opportunity even of knowing that his right is placed in jeopardy. A decision is made, is communicated to him and he either has to leave the government service altogether or is transferred to what is called a less sensitive position. That is not the system which is followed in other jurisdictions. There the civil servant is given the fullest opportunity of knowing the nature of the case against him, is asked if he wishes to make any explanation and is afforded the opportunity to make an explanation. There are tribunals set up before which the suspected person can appear and, as I have pointed out in an earlier quotation, in the United Kingdom there has been quite a substantial number of reinstatements as the result of the suspected person being given the opportunity to explain the situation on the basis of which he has come under suspicion and to produce a satisfactory explanation for the associations which he has made or other circumstances which have given rise to the suspicion.
I will conclude at this point, although I shall have more to say at a later stage, by
Supply-Justice
summarizing in this way. There can be no disagreement, I take it, that the government is under the very heavy obligation of ensuring the loyalty of the public service of Canada. However, I have given reasons why I believe that we have no cause to be satisfied at the present time that they are efficiently and vigorously discharging that obligation. We are not given any facts upon which we can base any such conclusion, and I have referred the committee to two or three examples from the past on the basis of which I suggest we have cause for uncertainty and dissatisfaction, because they are examples of past carelessness.
But, on the other hand, we have no assurance that whatever measures they do take are taken with fairness to the individual because, on the basis of the system as outlined by the ministers themselves, there exist these two particular features which carry with them, inevitably and inescapably, the element of unfairness. This element, I submit can be overcome by working out a method of appeal procedure along the lines that have been suggested previously, along lines which are suggested by the setting up of these procedures in other jurisdictions, particularly in the United Kingdom.
Before sitting down there is a correction I should like to make because I do not want to leave a wrong impression. When I was referring to the fact that Sam Carr had not had his certificate of naturalization revoked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration asked me in the course of my remarks whether it was alleged that Carr had acquired his certificate by fraud. As I recall it, I said that the report of the royal commission indicated that. I do not want to leave the impression that the report of the royal commission states as a fact that Carr acquired his naturalization certificate by fraud. What they do is to make it abundantly clear that at the time when he was granted the certificate in 1945 he was engaged vigorously in espionage activities. It is my own conclusion following from that, and on the basis of the answer that the minister gave to the written question-that he got the certificate on the basis of an allegation of loyalty to Canada and to His Majesty-that obviously he acquired it as the result of a fraudulent declaration.

I wonder whether the minister has any comments to make on the matter. The minister still refuses to agree that there is justification for giving factual

information as to the number of cases thus far dealt with and the disposition of those cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I differ from
my hon. friend in what he has just said.

For what reasons does the
minister differ?

For reasons that have been

speechtext: Reasons of secrecy!

Will the minister explain how he can reconcile his position with the fact that in the United Kingdom they give totals and break down the disposition of those totals without naming names-that is not asked for here-without doing any prejudice to the individual? If that can be done there how does it follow that it cannot be done here without giving rise to prejudice against the individual?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
