Is there some difference in human nature between the people of this country and the people in other countries? Is there some factor which would dictate a difference in policy?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Macleod.

With respect, Mr. Chairman, I have asked the minister questions which are reasonable and which I think deserve an answer. I have given the background for my questions and they are based on fact. I am not content to have the minister sit silent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know that the hon. gentleman is just as concerned as we are, Mr. Chairman, about the proper administration of security measures in this country. He asks if there is any difference between human nature in this country and human nature in other countries. I believe that is a rather rhetorical question. Of course there is no difference in human nature in this country and human nature in other countries. It so happens, however, that this government is responsible for the administration of security measures in this country and is not responsible for the administration of security measures in other countries. I am sure that the hon. member is doing his best to serve the interests of his fellow citizens. I hope he would be generous enough to think we too are doing our best.
It may be that we are making mistakes, but we are doing our best to balance this difficult equation between the security of the classified information that has to be available in some branches of the service, and

fairness to the individual. The hon. gentleman speaks about there being conviction and of there being exoneration as a result of appeals. I think that is not quite the question. No doubt the right to earn one's living is a right that it is damaging to take from anyone, but there is no inherent right in anyone to enjoy my confidence for confidential services in assisting me in discharging the responsibilities for which I am the one who is responsible to parliament and to the Canadian people.
This matter of reliance upon someone else with respect to confidential relations is not something that is determined on the basis of there being guilt or innocence. It is a matter of appreciation. The hon. gentleman is still exercising a profession that it was my privilege to exercise for a great many years. There is no obligation upon anyone in the community to employ him, any more than there was any obligation upon anyone in the community to employ me. It was only if they had confidence in an individual that they went to him for confidential advice and confidential assistance.
These matters are matters with which it is extremely delicate to deal, and about which we are just as careful as we can be; careful of the feeling that in our selection of confidential assistants we are taking every possible precaution to avoid the divulging of anything that is required to be kept secret. This does not involve only a question of loyalty, but it involves a question of there being solidity of character and discretion in the persons who are placed in that confidential relationship. There cannot be any question of exonerating someone about whom serious and honest doubts exist in the mind of the one who happens to be responsible for whatever is done by that one individual in assisting him in discharging his public responsibilities.
It is not a question of guilt or exoneration. It is a question of the degree of confidence one is prepared to place in an individual. Fortunately there are not many troublesome cases. There are some. The hon. gentleman says that up to 1950 we did disclose the numbers. There were two occasions when that was done, as the hon. member knows. There was a great and rather general anxiety about the film board in 1949 and 1950, to such an extent that the Department of National Defence was not entrusting its classified films to the film board. It was decided, therefore, that there would be a thorough screening of everyone in the film board.
When the minister made his report to parliament I believe he said some 580 files had

been carefully scrutinized, and there had been a few separations from the board required as a result of that incident. He did say then for the purpose of satisfying the public that there was not anything very serious the matter with the film board; that only three out of 580 odd had been found to be such that their separation from the board was required in order to restore full confidence in the security of information that might be imparted by work entrusted to the film board.
Then there was another question that came up a short time afterwards as to the number who had been separated for security reasons from the national research council. There was no reason whatever to refrain from giving that information. There were only two, and they had been prosecuted and convicted. Those were facts that already were public. We were very happy to be able to say there were no others. I would be very happy if I could say that since that time there have been no others anywhere in the public service, but I am not in a position to say that. There have not been very many in the civil service. There have been quite a number who had been enrolled in the armed services without having been screened, and when they were screened were found to be persons that it was felt preferable not to have in the armed forces. But in the civilian departments of government there have not been very many. There have been many cases of consideration as to whether someone who was not in a confidential relationship, not in a position where he had access to classified material should be placed in such a position. But that is something about which no statistics can be maintained.
If there is any doubt at all about the advisability of putting someone into a confidential relationship who has not had that relationship before-well, nothing happens. I have been quite concerned about this, and I have tried to get information-
I hope you do not have the same difficulty I have had.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As a matter of fact I did have some difficulty, but perhaps not for the same reason. I did have some difficulty because there has been no compilation made of those who have been either not transferred to some other position because there was some doubt about them or those who have been transferred to some other position because there was some uneasiness about the possibility of their divulging information, either through motives of disloyalty or other reasons for possible indiscretions.
Supply-Justice
There has been no tabulation kept of that. I can understand that where they have a system regarding this as some kind of trial which has to take place before some kind of special board, there may be exact mathematical computations of the number of cases that come before that board, and there is possible a mathematical determination of what proportion is dealt with in one way and what proportion is dealt with in another way. Rightly or wrongly we have not felt that that was desirable, unless there is something that appears to us to justify a conviction. We try to avoid the possibility of leaks, without there being anything concretely determined about it.
There can be all sorts of examples. There is no guilt by association; but sometimes there is information about association that does disturb us. It is unfortunate, but I think we have to assume that there are efforts made by foreign powers to obtain through their espionage or intelligence services information that we think they should not have. And we have to be on our guard against the possibility of their furthering their purposes.
Are our measures fully effective? No one could say that, except those to whom these possible agents or others would make their reports; and we cannot get information from them. But we do assume that they are making efforts to get this kind of information, and we feel that we have to be on our guard There are personal files for all those who are in any confidential capacity, and all sorts of information becomes available and has to be_ considered. And whenever there is anything that appears to be derogatory in any way, because of character, because of the possible susceptibility to blackmail and because of social contacts, well, we have to appraise all that.
Fortunately it does not often make us feel that our responsibility requires action, and there has not been any case where we have been put in possession of material that would justify prosecution, though there have been some bits of information that might have been sufficient to make a case. But that would require disclosing the sources from which this information was obtained; and I think that that would be very detrimental to our counter-intelligence activities. I think that it is very necessary for all our counterintelligence activities that they be not publicized. They have to be secret in order to be effective.
Now, we did give serious consideration to the possibility of having some kind of appeal, and we came to the conclusion that we were better able to discharge our responsibility

Supply-J ustice
in that regard under the present system. We never refuse to reconsider a question; but we endeavour to exhaust everything that would be available on any kind of appeal, except, of course, saying to the individual, "I am sorry, but I feel that I can no longer rely upon you because of such and such a thing. What have you got to say?" That we have not felt would be the proper procedure, because that would make it an accusation, and we are not accusing anyone; any more than I felt I was being accused when someone who had been my client went to some other lawyer. I felt that it was his business to place his confidence wherever he considered he should do so. This matter of confidence in the reliability of others is not something that can be decided as a result of a trial. We have to be honest with others, but we have also to be honest with ourselves. And we try to keep ourselves surrounded by persons in whom individually we have implicit confidence.
With respect to unfairness about others, we are extremely cautious, even when it is possible to find some less sensitive position worth as much money. Because it may well be that if someone is taken out of a line of service for which he prepared himself, and which he intended to make his career, though he may get the same remuneration in some other job, it is still unfortunate to have to do anything like that. And we do our best to be fair. I do not think the hon. member, or any other member of parliament, has heard of any concrete case where unfairness was actually experienced, or where one felt that unfairness had been imposed upon any individual. Perhaps the hon. gentleman feels that the whole system is unfair; but the hon. gentleman must realize that it is not easy to maintain that balance. We may be wrong, but we do not think it would be better maintained by setting up any established and recognized security board to make decisions.
The hon. member has spoken about a security panel, and asked whether the Secretary of State was a member of it.
Of the secretariat.

He asked if the Secretary of State had been secretary, and he said he had not been. The hon. member asked if the Secretary of State was still a member of the board. I think it has been made clear in the former statements that have been made here that this panel is an interdepartmental committee of officials. There is no member of the government on the panel, and there is no requirement that whatever anxiety any minister or deputy minister

may have about any individual shall go to the panel. It is the minister and the deputy minister who are responsible for the department.
They sometimes have recourse to the panel for the purpose of securing advice of those we have implicit confidence in because of the positions they occupy in the service, and the experience we have had with them while they were in the service. The declarations that have been made show, in a general way, how that interdepartmental committee is made up, and I do not think that the hon. gentleman feels there would be anything of value in disclosing at any particular moment the names of the officials who happened at that time to be members of the panel. They make no decisions; they simply tender advice and of course they do not deal only with the screening of individuals. They deal with the many and varied aspects of our counterintelligence service and consider and advise on the sufficiency of the measures that are taken with respect to those matters. I think that our efforts for the protection of the secrecy of our classified material have been successful. That of course is a matter of opinion because we were quite as surprised as anyone could be at the revelations which took place in 1945.
We have been possibly more careful, but we cannot be sure that, careful as we have been, we have been 100 per cent successful. That is something about which we cannot have accurate information. If we were to attempt to state figures we would have to go through a very large number of files, because there are many occasions where the possibility of indiscretion, the possibility of there being disloyalty, is one factor about which we are perhaps a little bit uncertain, but there develops some other obvious and plausible reasons for a change, and the change is made and made with all the appearance as having been made for other than security anxieties. I am not saying that we falsely represent, even to ourselves, why the change is being made, but this other situation is such that the change would probably be made anyway, and because we have not been too happy over the situation, a change will be made.
How would that be classified? Just as an illustration-I do not think it fits any case, so I can perhaps use it-suppose there is the case of a young office boy who is used for the purpose of delivering packets, and the question arises as to whether he could be used for the delivery of packets that would contain classified material. A special screening is made. Well, suppose it develops that we find that unfortunately there had been occasions

where there had been pilfering. Well, he certainly would not get the job that would put him in a position where he could have in his possession classified material. Would that be a security case, or would it be otherwise counted?
The statement of a certain number of figures would certainly not mean anything unless we were able to elaborate and to describe the cases to which these figures applied. In the two instances that the hon. gentleman referred to the situation was quite different. There was no possible objection and no possible reason for not disclosing them. There had been two employees of the national research council who had been prosecuted under the Official Secrets Act, had been found guilty and had been dismissed.
The hon. gentleman proceeds from the same premises that we proceed from. The system should be efficient in protecting the secrecy of what should be kept secret. It should be such as not to be unfair to individuals about whom any decision has to be made. It is in the application of those principles that the hon. gentleman feels there would be advantage in more publicity. We do not think that is so. I do not think the hon. gentleman really believes that we are refraining from making disclosures because we feel it would be embarrassing to the government. I do not see how it could be embarrassing to the government unless we were compelled to disclose that we are taking the kind of risks that we are unwilling to take. It certainly would be embarrassing to have to admit that we were taking calculated risks in a matter susceptible to such consequences as the maintaining of proper security of classified material.
It must not be overlooked, you know, that we belong to the NATO organization, and that we exchange a lot of classified information with our allies. Even if we could take the responsibility of calculated risks for ourselves, we certainly could not take any responsibility for calculated risks for classified information coming from other sources, or we would very soon cease getting that classified information. That does not mean that our affairs are being run by others, but it does mean that we assure our allies that we take every possible precaution and that we do not consider that everyone who has not been convicted is entitled to be trusted with this confidential information.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Kamloops will permit me, I interjected something when he was speaking this morning which may have been misleading. I have not had any connection with the secretariat of 83276-345
Supply-Justice
the security panel, but I was, as I think is quite notorious, the chairman of the security panel for something over a year.

We are grateful to the Secretary of State for giving us information which was refused on a former occasion.
I appreciate the attitude of the Prime Minister and the careful way in which he has dealt with this matter. I agree the whole question is one of great concern, one which we should try to handle on the basis that it is of equal concern to all of us. If in a matter of this kind there are objections and differences of opinion then the objections can best be met and the differences can best be resolved with benefit to the nation by being discussed, with moderation on either side.
I am therefore glad the Prime Minister has taken this occasion to place before us so clearly those considerations which influence the government in deciding to continue unmodified, so far at any rate, its course of policy in dealing with this matter, so that they can be discussed fully.
There are one or two statements which the Prime Minister has made which indicate that we on this side have not perhaps made clear our approach to the matter and our suggestion as to how it may be dealt with. I hope we can make our views clear and the government will then be willing to reconsider again whether there is not some merit for what we say and some justification therefore on their part for modifying the present procedure.
The Prime Minister has based his case on the principle in part that no one has an absolute right to employment, particularly in a position with security implications. He has drawn a parallel between the employment of a civil servant and the retention by a client of a solicitor. He has pointed out that no solicitor has a right to continue to be retained by a client by whom he has been retained on a previous occasion. But, with respect, I do not think the parallel is apt.
The civil servant has made a choice which involves many sacrifices. We have always agreed, in the past at any rate, that remuneration in the public service is not on the same level generally speaking with remuneration in private employment. It is true they have some recompense for that. There is what we call security of tenure, and there used to be some pension privileges which did not exist in private employment. The civil servant has therefore made his choice and embarked on a career; he is committed to a course. I know the Prime Minister did not intend that his analogy should be taken too

Supply-Justice
literally and I do not wish to emphasize the point too much, but I think there is a very wide difference between the matter of selection which is exercised each time a client chooses a solicitor, and the permanence of the choice made by a civil servant. While I agree in strict fact that he has no irrevocable right to be continued in that employment, we on this side maintain he cannot be removed from that employment without the strictest proof possible that he is no longer qualified to continue in that employment.
Now, if that be the case-and that seems to me to be a matter of simple justice, on the basis of good relations alone, if you like, between the two sides-it seems to me that you cannot lightly dispense with the services of a man-though I am not suggesting it is done-who has dedicated himself to the public service and has perhaps been there for ten years. The problem therefore seems to me to be one of approach and we would place more emphasis on the necessity of maintaining that person in the public service, not up to the point where the public interest is going to be prejudiced, but simply as to where suspicion as to his suitability has been aroused so that the process of exhausting every possibility in his defence will be thoroughly carried out; so that that man may be given an opportunity to explain his position; after which the decision and the ultimate responsibility will have to be exercised.
The Prime Minister has stated that it may be that I take objection to this system on the basis that it is inherently unfair. It is true that I do so in part, and I think it could be made less inherently unfair. But I also take objection to it on the basis of the experience of one case within my knowledge where there was unfairness, and another case where, I admit, I have nothing but suspicion to go on, but it appears to me to be very suspicious. In the first case, the man involved does not even know the case against him. It is only by reason of a lengthy discussion with him myself that we have decided that it must be on grounds of security. We could be wrong, but in my opinion the conclusion is inescapable, though he has not been told that he was under suspicion in connection with security. He was not brought in and interviewed and told that certain facts seemed to require an explanation.
He has given me an explanation which seems to me to meet the situation and with which any reasonable person would be satisfied. He was not a highly placed civil servant in charge of confidential work, and in fact I think it would be fair to describe him as a rather junior employee. No reason was

given to him for his services being dispensed with and he cannot go to another employer without references. One can imagine what would happen. "Where did you last work? Why did you leave?" He would have to answer: "I do not know. They told me my services were no longer required."
That man has a choice. He has, I suppose, a right to make a public issue of the matter and bring his name before the public and let it be known that he fell under suspicion because of certain activities with a security implication. He says he thinks he can explain the matter and indeed he is convinced he can explain it satisfactorily, namely, that the association which previously existed no longer exists, and did not exist, incidentally, at the time his services were dispensed with. He can do that, or he can accept the situation because there is no procedure by which he can appeal, no procedure by which he can bring his case before the authorities and have a hearing before the authorities in person.
It is my desire, while still emphasizing the necessity of taking these measures which will protect the security of the public service, to work out a procedure within that general aim which will satisfy us as being as fair as it can be so that we can say to those who apply these security tests that they can be rigorously and vigorously employed because we have protected the individual, given him a fair hearing, and they can now go ahead and apply the policy as vigorously as they wish. I am not suggesting that any board be set up which would in itself make a decision. I am prepared to go along, at the moment at any rate, with the Prime Minister when he said on a former occasion that the ultimate decision as to whether a man is suitable must rest with the government. I am prepared to go along with the view that theirs is the responsibility; but I think there should be something in the nature of an intermediate board before which hearings could be held and to which a man would have an opportunity to state his case. That board could pass on its findings with respect to that hearing to the minister for his information at the time when he exercises his final decision.
That is the system which is followed in the United Kingdom. I hope I can make it very clear that I do not think that because it is done in the United Kingdom it has to be done here. It is not that at all. But I put this forward for consideration. The United Kingdom is, I should think, even more apt to feel the first Russian hydrogen bomb than we are. They are a lot closer and therefore they have just as much at stake in preserving the secrecy of secret information as we

545ft
have, and they seem to have been able to work out this procedure by which they feel they can protect their security interests and yet provide a method which will protect the sense of justice and fairness to the individual.
This method was evolved as long ago as 1948 when the Labour government was in power and, on the basis of the information I have been able to gather, I understand it is still being followed by the present government in the United Kingdom. I would therefore like to place on the record at some length a quotation from the British Hansard wherein Mr. Attlee outlined the procedure in a debate on March 25, 1948. He said, and this is to be found at columns 3421 to 3423 inclusive:
Suppose there Is a case in which there is room to suspect disloyalty. The first thing to be done is to see that the civil servant concerned is informed. He should not be merely informed that he is suspected, but should be given, as far as possible, chapter and verse, saying, "You are a member of this organization, you did this or that, can you explain it?" He ought to have the case put before him perfectly clearly. Secondly he must be given the opportunity of studying that case, and then given the opportunity of putting in his reply, and also of making his reply. That then goes before the departmental head, who must consider whether it is a matter in which action must be taken. He must then go to the minister, and, whatever we think of ministers, they have a pretty fair knowledge of psychology, as they have been in this house for some time. They will have a broad view; we have to take a broad view of these things. They will look at the whole of the evidence and consider whether or not there is a prima facie case for transferring this man on these grounds or, it may be, even for dismissing him.
Then we want something beyond the minister to assist him. We are, therefore, proposing a further safeguard. We are setting up an advisory body of three retired civil servants. I hope to give the names some time, and I am quite sure they will be names which will inspire confidence in the civil service. If the minister considers there is a prima facie case, he will send the whole of the evidence before this body. Before this body the person concerned will be able to appear and make his case. He will also be able to ask other people to speak for him. The whole of this will be sifted very carefully, wherever the information comes from, by this advisory body; and the advisory body will then send their advice to the minister. The minister will then have to decide on the whole of the case as to whether he takes their advice, or rejects their advice, or what action he proposes to take. That, I think, gives the opportunity people ought to have of stating their case.
Then the prime minister of Britain went on to say this, and this is a point that has been raised here, and I think he dealt with it fairly effectively:
It is quite impossible-and everyone will realize that it is

that we should give in detail exactly the sources of information. If we do that, we destroy anything like an effective security service. But it is our intention to do this with the greatest possible tenderness for the individual, consistent with the security of the community and, as I have said, the security of the fellow members of the civil service.
Supply-Justice
Then a little bit later in that same debate he was asked a question by Mr. Brown as follows:

I wish to thank the prime minister for his statement, but I would like to ask whether it would be within the competence of the proposed advisory body of retired civil servants to send, not only for the papers that would be supplied, but also for the man himself?
The Prime Minister: I think that is quite clear. He would certainly appear.
Hence under that system-and I am not just saying it is a good system because it happens to be in effect there; I am saying that I think it is a good system because it does seem to protect the individual against possible injustice-the individual has the opportunity of knowing the nature of the case against him.
It may be that there was an unwise association in the past which has come to light. It may be that it is a perfectly innocent association. There may be a perfectly simple explanation for that association and one which-if the explanation were ever asked for or an opportunity afforded for it to be given -would satisfy the authorities that there is; no security risk here, that all that needs to be done is to draw to the attention of the person that this is an undesirable association and the matter will rest there. But in the case I have in mind there was no such opportunity to explain. One could also imagine other cases where there is a simple and satisfactory explanation which could be made were the basis of the suspicion known to the suspected person. I am convinced that under the present procedure followed here- indeed it has been stated that it is not the general practice to inform the civil servant that he is under suspicion or the reasons for the suspicion-in general there can be no opportunity of meeting the case afforded to the man who is suspected, however innocent he may be. I do not like to think that sort of principle and procedure is followed here in Canada. That is my point.
With respect to the type of appeal, or intermediate hearing and procedure-to which I have referred, and which is afforded in the United Kingdom, I believe that the nature of the case could be stated to the individual concerned without the revelation of any particular piece of information which would enable a genuinely disloyal person to trace and to break down the security system. I do not think facts and dates need necessarily be given with particularity nor need the source of the information be given. Indeed, in the United Kingdom Mr. Attlee made it clear that there must be limitations upon the right of the suspected person to know all the information. He referred to a number of

Supply-Justice
cases which were brought to his attention by the association over there which looks after civil service matters. He told them: I said at the outset that I did not mean that every piece of information, including the sources, in our possession, would be made available but rather an outline of the case with as much particularity as possible; and he repeated that what would be done was to inform the suspect of the nature of the case against him with as much particularity as possible having regard to the necessity to protect their own security system.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is that system still in effect under the present British government?

My information is that the
same system is at present in effect. Indeed it was Mr. Butler who gave the latest figures as to the number of cases dealt with under that system and the results. I can see the reason for the doubts and for the care which would have to be exercised but I can see no insuperable obstacle to the implementation of a similar system here in Canada so that we can demand with confidence-and it is our duty to demand; it is the government's duty to discharge the responsibility-the most vigorous and effective enforcement of a policy of security, secure ourselves in the knowledge, as would be the government, that as far as it is humanly possible to ensure it, no individual is going to be unjustly prejudiced as a result of the application of that policy.

Mr. Chairman, without breaking the continuity of discussion that has taken place today, I should like to say just a word on this matter. I do so somewhat reluctantly after listening to the Prime Minister. I want to assure him that I believe when he was speaking every hon. member in this committee was conscious of the fact that he was doing so with conviction, with sincerity and with honesty of purpose in the discharge of the heavy responsibilities that rest upon him in these particular days. That is the way I felt, and I am sure every other hon. member of the committee will agree with me.
There is, however, a phase that I should like to take up this afternoon. There is no question about it that we are living in extremely tense times. We are living in days the like of which human history has never before witnessed. To my mind there are two realms in which the enemy of mankind is at work. One is in the realm of physics which in these days is expressing itself in the scientific realm, where there is a danger which is so great that it threatens the survival of the human race. That is one realm in which the enemy is at work.

There is another realm, the realm of the human mind and the human personality. In that respect I refer to what some of us hold as a very deep conviction, the basic freedom of individual man. The enemy is at work in both these fields, and living in such times as we do, witnessing the things that are happening in the world and at the highest possible level of world affairs, there is no question that anyone who is interested at all must be interested to the point of being alarmed. We read of investigations being carried on in other countries, particularly the United States. We cannot help but be influenced by the result of some of these investigations, and it would be inconceivable and the height of stupidity for anyone to conclude that the same espionage forces that have been at work there have forgotten all about Canada. They just have not. Yet when we ask about the matter, and I do not want to be too harsh, we are politely told that it is well in hand and that we must therefore trust the government.
I go a long way in trusting the government with such responsibility but I must confess that I do not know very much about the situation and I do not think I am different from any other hon. member. I must confess I should like to know something about it. I am not interested in some individual case here and there but I am certainly interested in the methods that are being pursued. I do not know if it was news to other hon. members but it was news to me that the Secretary of State was the chairman of that security panel. I doubt whether anyone knew that. We are told that to reveal any steps that are being taken might possibly incriminate some innocent person. I have the greatest sympathy for those who are attempting to manage the affairs of the country and who do not wish to cast any reflection upon the character or integrity of any person. I think everybody in the house sympathizes with that position, but just the same I do believe that in many cases it can be used as a sort of red herring drawn across the trail, a red herring which is sometimes labelled "guilt by association".
I realize there is a principle involved there and that the greatest of care must be taken. I call it a red herring because I believe that is exactly what it is. I do not know of anyone who has actually been declared to be guilty of anything just because he piay have been friendly with a person who was vitally involved. Nevertheless there is a principle, and I think the principle is largely one of personal responsibility. I can think of it in a rather light vein. I am a clergyman by

ordinary profession. I have to watch my step. If I went downtown and were seen entering a pub I might be able to come out and tell one of my elders whom I met on the street that I went in to see a man.
You might not be able to come out.

I might be able to argue that I was in there trying to convert men from the errors of their ways. However, if 1 were seen going in there regularly I might not be guilty of anything but I could not very well blame my board of elders if they asked for my resignation. After all, much of it boils down to personal responsibility, and sometimes steps have to be taken. Just the other day I was reading about the decision made by the board of men directed, I believe, by the President of the United States, to investigate the case of Dr. Oppenheimer. We all know the result. Dr. Oppenheimer, one of the greatest scientists of the day, from now on is denied secret information. Yet the board came out with the clear-cut statement that they believed that Dr. Oppenheimer was a loyal citizen of the United States. I believe he is.
Not long ago I talked to a gentleman whose name I cannot tell you because he spoke to me in confidence, a man who had rubbed elbows with some of these great scientists. He said that clearly they live in a different world from us. He said that he can quite understand how in their associations they may come in contact with people who may be part of an espionage ring and yet they will not recognize it at all. Be that as it may, sometimes steps have to be taken because after all in these days we are not dealing merely with a man's position or job but with the possibility of the survival of the human race. We are dealing with the greatest of all fundamental freedoms, the freedom of individual man.
The system of espionage that is being used by the Russians, the enemies of our way of life, is so inconceivable and so fantastic that it pushes the wildest spy fiction of my teenage days completely into the background. That is why I say it is not merely a matter of somebody running off with some secrets or pilfering a diplomatic bag, it is a question of a system that has been devised to so permeate our way of life as to be able to engineer men of the highest possible intellectual calibre into positions at the highest level where those men have actually influenced government policy. There is no question about that.
I only have to refer to the person of Harry Dexter White, who became assistant treas-
Supply-Justice
urer of the United States. He had a tremendous power that affected the economic destinies of the nation. There is no question in my mind but that the debauching of the currency of China was part of a scheme. While I cannot put my finger on any particular spot, there is no question in my mind but that the same evil powers had designs on wrecking the United Kingdom economy. I must say it is only because of the integrity and stamina of the English-speaking people, and their leadership through the times, that they have been able to come through and apparently come out on top.
It is this matter of the influencing of government policy at the highest level that is significant to my way of thinking. I have a newspaper clipping here. I am sorry I cannot give the date of it, but it cannot be very long ago because I never keep these clippings too long. I believe I clipped it from a paper giving a summary of the news, and the heading is, "U.S. Reds Strong, F.B.I. Chief says." It goes on to say:
The United States communist party has "strong fifth column strength", federal bureau of investigation director J. Edgar Hoover has told the House of Representatives appropriations committee.
Hoover's comments to the committee-which was considering F.B.I. estimates for the coming fiscal year-were made recently in private. They were released February 6.
Hoover listed the following as objectives of the American communist party:
Settlement of the Korean war; recall of American troops from abroad: a five-power peace pact including communist China: resumption of U.S. trade with iron curtain nations.
Let us make note of the last point. It is the matter of influencing of government policy, which policy is tied in with the destiny of the nation, that gives some of us extreme concern.
In another debate yesterday I referred to a recent report that has been made by the commission set up by the Australian government to look into the Petrov case. I have here a news dispatch, which I suppose all hon. members have read dated May 18, I believe, giving an analysis of that somewhat preliminary report. I am not going to read a great deal of it, but I should like to read a part of it. It says:
Petrov and his agents painstakingly collected details about the personal lives of various persons and sent them to Moscow. The dockets included their relations with women, their drinking habits, whether they were short of money, whether they could be inveigled into talking, and their political leanings.
Other scandalous material became known about Australians' private lives, this was held for its blackmail value-to put the heat on those who might become involved directly or indirectly with the soviet intelligence system.

I could read on, but the report is there for anyone to read. It is not, therefore, merely a matter of the stealing of secrets involved in nuclear energy or something of that kind. It is more than that. They work upon human nature. There is not a person living v/hose personality or whose human nature has no chinks through which he could be reached in some or any of these ways which are so cleverly and subtly designed. It is for that reason we have to be so very careful.
I am not going to repeat the request of the hon. member for Kamloops. I shall have another suggestion to make about that, but I believe the Prime Minister should tell us something about the activities of the R.C.M.P., the organization charged with dealing with communism in Canada. I have a report here of April 29, 1954. I suppose the minister has read it. In an interview a former member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police stated that there are between 8,000 and 9,000 card-bearing communists in Canada at present, and when sympathizers and fellow travellers are counted the total might exceed 50,000. The point I wanted to make was that he said there were schools inaugurated and being carried on throughout Canada, and that the leaders in some of these schools are trained in Moscow. The article reads as follows:
The national school was held annually at a location about 100 miles from Toronto, he said. Provincial schools were held several times a year to Indoctrinate new members. The party also operated a summer school each year at Sylvan lake in Alberta.
In addition there were local study groups and schools for adults and children in Montreal, Ottawa, Windsor, Toronto and Winnipeg, as well as other centres. Toronto was headquarters for the largest organized groups but Winnipeg for years had been the centre for a "virile" communist organization.
These are local study groups and schools for adults and children. I believe we should have some sort of report about that from the minister, since his estimates are before us.
I do not want to keep the house any longer, Mr. Chairman, but the Prime Minister must not feel too badly if there is an indication from many members of their extreme concern about this, shall I say,

philosophical espionage system in Canada that attempts to capture the minds of men towards their philosophy, and lead Canada astray in respect to its highest level policy making.
That is what I am personally concerned about. Because once it is done you cannot retreat from your position. I do not know how long our present government is going to be in office, but one thing is certain: They are on their way out, because that is the only way they can go.

And some other responsible leaders are going to take their place. When I go through the country I say to the people, "I am not going to be too harsh on the Liberal government, but it has to be changed some time. You do not suppose there is going to be a Liberal government here a hundred years from now, do you"?

speechtext: New faces, perhaps.

I am saying that one government builds upon another. The work of one government cannot always be retrieved. It is not just a matter of coming here for a session of parliament, getting up and talking, drawing our pay and going home. We represent the people, and our responsibility is toward the destiny of this nation. Is the nation going to follow the line of least resistance, or are we going to emerge a virile nation, a God-fearing nation of men and women with honesty and integrity of purpose, a nation as free as God intended men should be, when He created them in the likeness of His own image?

Mr. Chairman, under this vote I, too, desire to discuss a phase of security, a phase slightly different from that which has been under discussion for several hours. I do not know just how far the Minister of Justice can go in answering what I have in mind, but I sincerely hope he will go as far as possible in removing some of the confusion which exists in the minds of many people in Canada, and which I can say definitely exists at the moment in my own mind.
I shall introduce what I have to say in this way: A few years ago I had read of a nationally-known communist in eastern Canada. Being nationally-known he held a pretty high position in the communist organization. I gather that to get to a high position in a communist organization one has to

be dogmatic, a strict follower of the party line, something of a rabble-rouser, and definitely a revolutionary in their sense of the term. This man resigned in 1953 from the communist party and received a great deal of publicity throughout the length and breadth of this country in the press. I have been interested in having brought to my attention by a number of people remarks he made this year in the province of Quebec at a public meeting. I am referring to a man named Pat Walsh. The Quebec daily newspaper, L'Action Catholique, in its issue of Tuesday, January 26, quoted Mr. Walsh as follows:
I believe the time has come for me to reveal that when I took part in communist manifestations or when I was connected with communist organizations I was secretly working for the Department of Justice in Ottawa. At the time of my public resignation in February 1953 I had agreed with the authorities of the Department of Justice not to reveal this fact in order not to compromise the secret work of other agents inside the communist organizations. But today circumstances have changed and 1 have decided to reveal the fact that in reality I have always been a secret agent working for the central power.
I have taken this matter up with the Department of Justice. It is my understanding that it is the policy of the department when statements of this kind are made that neither the department nor the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will declare whether or not they are true. If that is so, perhaps there is a good explanation for it which, I am sure, the minister will give. If it is so, then I think first of all there is danger in allowing men with the past record and reputation of this man to make statements of that kind. I believe there is a danger there.
But my second point is perhaps more important, that if the information is correct, has consideration been given to whether or not a wrong policy is being followed in this matter of security, as it is related to a knowledge of communist activities? I can clearly and completely understand why, for purposes of security, the Department of Justice would like to have men placed in what they consider to be subversive organizations, to find out what is going on. Undoubtedly they have such men; the case of Sergeant Leopold proves that conclusively.
However, to reach the position of national importance in the communist organization in this country one would have to prove himself a good communist. He would have to persuade people in the Dominion of Canada to change their loyalty from this country to another, to accept a party and policy line from outside this country. In other words, to reach a position of that kind, you would have to be a successful evangelist of communism, and convert the democratic people of Canada to
Supply-Justice
communism. If it is correct that he was an agent of the federal department, then the government itself was employing a man to do the very thing we want to overthrow.
To me the whole situation is intriguing and at the same time confusing. It is a point upon which we should be given some clarification, and within the realm of security the minister should go as far as possible to inform us in the matter. Here we have a statement made by a man known formally as an avowed communist that he was at all times an agent of the Department of Justice. No denial is forthcoming, and we are told it cannot be forthcoming. Yet in the same month, in an issue of the Globe and Mail of January 13, we read about a man named Captain J. H. De Graff, allegedly a former Russian and British espionage agent.
In this report the R.C.M.P. are quoted as saying-and this is in quotation marks-that Captain De Graff is the genuine article; that he is a big operator, and that he served for three years in Montreal with the R.C.M.P. who knew him simply as Captain Johnny X. Here is a statement from the R.C.M.P. that another man was for three years working with the department as a secret service operator. Now that can be correct or incorrect, or perhaps the R.C.M.P. never made any such statement, although it is in quotation marks in the newspaper column. But it has never been denied, as far as I know, nor have the R.C.M.P. stated that they never made any such statement.
In one case there is no denial that they ever said this man was a secret service agent. Therefore he can get away with the statement the same as a former communist can get away with it when he makes a public speech in the province of Quebec. I think, sir, you cannot put both of them together and make them coincide. There must be some basis of policy as far as the Department of Justice is concerned in cases like this; and in view of the fact we have in one month two different men making this claim, it is of some importance and should be considered.
If possible I should like to hear from the minister just what is the policy as far as statements by his department or by the R.C.M.P. are concerned, on statements of this nature, and also what is the policy as regards the production of information or the production of files? Is there any, or has there been a definite policy, or is it strictly a matter of expediency under the circumstances of the case? Perhaps it might even go to political purposes. I am not saying anything about the actions of my hon. friend but I do know that in the past it was most difficult to understand the policy operations of the R.C.M.P.

Supply-Justice
I can very well remember, Mr. Chairman, when Canada was at war with Japan, the Japanese Canadians were moved off the Pacific coast. There were certain activities, commissions and advisory boards in British Columbia on this matter of the Japanese. A great many felt that there was one man in British Columbia who, instead of being left fairly loose just outside Lillooet, I think it was at Minto, should have been interned because the feeling there amongst the Japanese was that he had his loyalty in Japan, that he was a member of a national organization in Japan, that he was the British Columbia representative. The feeling and the pressure got to the point where the federal government made an investigation.
A learned judge was appointed to make the inquiry. I appeared, sir, before that inquiry on the stand and under oath. Why was I called? Because I had in my possession two copies of a newspaper that was printed in Japan in which this man's photograph appeared, and there was a write-up on him. These two papers were what we would term fascist organs; they were the official organs of a fascist national organization in Japan. I had these two magazines translated, and so I was called about the actual newspapers and the translation. At that inquiry it was asked whether the R.C.M.P. would produce their file on this man. Their file was of interest, and an inquiry was sent to the Department of Justice. The answer came back that the R.C.M.P. did not have the authority and could not get the authority for the production of this file. So, there was a file asked for from the R.C.M.P. on a matter that was being investigated, and it was denied. Nobody asked to produce any file on me but the counsel of the commission produced the secret service reports on me without being asked. That was the first time I knew I was being dogged and my utterances were being taken down by an agent of the R.C.M.P., and it was produced in that inquiry. Not that I am ashamed of anything I say at any time, and they can dog me all they like and they can take down every word I say and it will not bother me one bit. I do not take off my hat in this House of Commons to any man or woman or to any man or woman in Canada in my love of and loyalty to this Dominion of Canada.
What I am speaking about is this matter of production of files and giving of information. I think, sir, on this phase I have said enough. The minister understands the confusion and disturbance about it. If there can oe a clear and explicit explanation of matters of this nature, as well as of matters that were raised by previous speakers, it will mean a great deal, it will be of great benefit

to all the people in the Dominion of Canada, because knowledge is a lot better than lack of knowledge or guessing or rumour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are interested readers here of my hon. friend's very excellent column in the Vancouver Province.
I guessed that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And as he was good enough in his column in the issue of Saturday, March 20, 1954, to give us quite an effective notice of motion of the matter that he was going to bring up today I was able, by reason of that fact, to ask the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for a report upon all the major relevant allegations that were contained in this newspaper column. But before I deal point by point with these allegations, let me say a word with regard to the general policy which is followed by the special branch of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police engaged in counter-espionage work.
I am sure that I do not need to explain in any great detail to the members of such a well-informed body as the House of Commons that counter-espionage is scarcely the exact equivalent of conducting a Sunday school class, and that the R.C.M.P. special branch necessarily employs from time to time those whom it thinks will serve its particular purposes. I am sure, moreover, that the members upon the least reflection will agree with us that it would be a grave error indeed to discuss here any of our activities in the special branch, and especially to admit or deny any allegations of sometimes irresponsible people claiming to have been in our employ.
We are all aware that the practice of espionage and counter-espionage, the contest between enemy nations to secure and to prevent the securing of intelligence involves the building up, as completely as possible, of a large mass of information; and oftentimes the answer in the affirmative or negative to some simple statement of fact may be the last item needed to complete the general pattern of, if I may use that figure of speech, the jig-saw puzzle which the intelligence department is trying to put together; and this last simple answer may finally determine what that whole pattern is.
In counter-espionage work there is therefore only one safe policy to follow, and that is the policy of complete reticence about our own counter-espionage and complete reticence in respect of the espionage against which we are trying to protect Canada. It is for that reason that we have consistently refused to say anything with regard to the allegations of gentlemen like Mr. Pat Walsh. I

must confess that when I read my hon. friend's column, the one in question to which 1 have just referred, I was a little taken aback by his allegation that we had departed from that policy in the Captain De Graff case, though I was very gratified when he said at the conclusion of his remarks concerning the Pat Walsh matter, and I quote from him, "that if this case stood alone the position of the Minister of Justice is quite understandable." I gather from his whole column that the part that was not so understandable to him was that we should take the position we did in connection with the Pat Walsh matter, and then in the Captain De Graff case we should make revelations or comments.
Now, the report which I get from the R.C.M.P. on the Captain De Graff case and which I submit to members of this house as being accurate is to the following effect, as are all the reports which I receive from the force.
My hon. friend from Vancouver East referred to newspaper reports in which the R.C.M.P. is alleged to have described Captain De Graff as "the genuine article" and further "he was for three years in regular duty in Montreal with the R.C.M.P." Hence my hon. friend charges the Department of Justice with giving information about a secret agent in this case while refusing it in the Walsh case.
Now, Mr. Chairman, to show that there has been no inconsistency in principle I think it is necessary to begin with to recapitulate the substance of information which I have already conveyed verbally to my hon. friend from Vancouver East, to the effect that Captain De Graff as long ago as 1951 began making public appearances under cover of the name of "Captain X", and received a certain amount of newspaper publicity for these appearances in which he described his work in the Russian and British intelligence services. We conceded that Captain De Graff was undoubtedly a man of considerable knowledge in this field. During this period beginning 1951 the R.C.M.P. was asked on many occasions to give some indication of the authenticity of his background, that is the authenticity of the background he had been claiming for himself. This the police consistently declined to do until Captain De Graff last January, as reported in the Ottawa Journal, January 12, voluntarily disclosed his true identity.
At that time the press again sought some indication from the police about Captain De Graff's reliability. I think it is important that I should emphasize that. What the press sought was some indication from the police S3276-346
Supply-J ustice
as to Captain De Graff's reliability as an expert in the field of secret intelligence work. Undoubtedly the press wished to reassure themselves that he was not an impostor. At that time the press was told in general terms that Captain De Graff did have a background of successful work in secret intelligence, but this comment referred only to his activities before his arrival in Canada, activities in which, as I indicated a moment ago, he had been claiming association with the Russian and British intelligence services.
So far as the commissioner has been able to discover, no spokesman at R.C.M.P. headquarters used the phrase which I think my hon. friend has used, namely, "the genuine article".
I was referring to the comment in the newspaper column.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite agree: What I am saying is that we did not use the phrase my hon. friend quoted from the newspaper column. In other words, the R.C.M.P. was not the source of the items in the newspaper columns to the effect that Captain De Graff was "the genuine article".
As to Captain De Graff's possible relations with the R.C.M.P., the public interest requires us to continue to maintain a policy that such matters are never publicly disclosed even if a person claims, as did Captain De Graff, and as Pat Walsh made claim, to have been a secret agent of the R.C.M.P., even when such a claim may have a surface appearance of truth.
I think it will be readily appreciated by all of us that any official confirmation by the police acknowledging such a relationship would have a direct and adverse effect upon Canadian interests. Moreover, inasmuch as the Prime Minister has stated today that we work in security matters with the security agents of our partner nations in NATO, for us to make statements of this sort would destroy that confidence in our reliability which these other nations must continue to have if there is going to be that degree of co-operation between our efforts that there should be.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I submit that our policy in these two cases has been quite consistent in that we have neither confirmed nor denied the statements attributed to Pat Walsh and to Captain De Graff that they were secret agents of the R.C.M.P.
Now, with regard to another matter-and I hope my hon. friend from Vancouver East will forgive me if I mispronounce a Japanese name-in the Morii case my hon. friend will recall his reference to the proceedings of the royal commission which was set up in

Supply-Justice
October 1942 under Mr. Justice J. C. A. Cameron of the exchequer court to inquire into a report of an allegation published in the Vancouver News-Herald to the effect that a black dragon society was active among the Japanese in British Columbia; and that one Etsuji Morii was connected with that society, and that the R.C.M.P. had been "complacent" in dealing with this gentleman. These newspaper articles particularly claimed that the force had been at fault in accepting this gentleman's services in arranging for evacuation of persons of Japanese descent from the west coast.
I think I should here insert parenthetically that the royal commission's report disposed of all these allegations as being unfounded, and described in detail the useful work of this gentleman for the Japanese community, for the Canadian government and for the R.C.M.P. with respect to this evacuation.
My hon. friend's article stated that the R.C.M.P. file on Morii was asked for by counsel of the Vancouver News-Herald and production of it was denied. My hon. friend from Vancouver East is quite correct in this statement. By telegram dated November 13, 1942, to the counsel for the R.C.M.P., former commissioner Wood wired as follows:
It is not considered in public interest nor has it been policy in past to produce confidential files as in case of Morii where frequent references are made to information received from secret service of other countries and thus lead to disclosure of identity of confidential informants (stop) Such action would be violation of undertaking given secret service of other countries.
That is in line with what I have stated to be our consistent policy and the policy which we have followed in the cases of Pat Walsh and Captain De Graff.
But my hon. friend's article goes on to allege a serious inconsistency in that, in spite of the rule with regard to the production of these files, a police file on my hon. friend himself was introduced as he says before the commission. My hon. friend's paragraph to this effect in his article is in these words:
Without any warning and without any request being made to counsel the federal government produced the R.C.M.P. file on myself. As a matter of fact, from this file they read into the record R.C.M.P. verbatim reports from the speeches I had made.
I regarded this as a rather serious affair- the allegation that we would not produce a file in one case and that we would produce a file on my hon. friend and read from such files speeches of his into the record of the royal commission. I therefore instructed that a careful search should be made of the proceedings of the royal commission. A search was made of all of the proceedings conducted

under Mr. Justice Cameron and also a search of his report to the then minister of justice. I must say, Mr. Chairman-and I say it with some embarrassment; I do not like to contradict my hon. friend from Vancouver East- that the fact is that there is no record whatever in either the proceedings or the commissioner's report that such a file was ever produced at that inquiry and much less that it was read into the record.
I can still remember the questioning.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is perhaps confusing the production of that report which did not take place and which was not read into the record with another episode. He may have recalled that a Sergeant J. K. Barnes, at that time head of the R.C.M.P. intelligence section at Vancouver, had stated in his testimony that my hon. friend as a member of an advisory board established by the government to give assistance to the security commission of the British Columbia government with regard to the evacuation of Japanese was permitted to address a group of Japanese who had complained about the treatment they were receiving from the R.C.M.P. My hon. friend was accompanied on that occasion by another member of the force, Constable Turner, who heard my hon. friend say, and so reported to Sergeant Barnes certain statements, which statements may have been the ones to which I think my hon. friend refers. But there was no report as my hon. friend alleges.
I hope that all of this will convince my hon. friend that there is some fairly substantial measure of consistency in the policy that we follow in this regard. I have always understood him to agree with us-and I hope he will correct me if I misunderstand him-that in the operation of a special branch or of any secret service activity there is only one policy that can be followed and that is complete reticence and complete non-production of files.
While I am on my feet I might perhaps refer to a matter which was raised by the hon. member for Macleod in quoting former superintendent Leopold with regard to the number of communists-that is the actual card-carrying members of the party-in Canada at the present time and also as to the number of fellow travellers or supporters of the communist party line. The figures my friend the hon. member for Macleod gave were between 8,000 and 9,000 for card-carrying members and 50,000 for the fellow travellers.
I might now point up that information by laying before the members of the committee

the fact that at the time former superintendent Leopold retired in July, 1952, he indicated at a press interview which had been arranged for him by the R.C.M.P. that he intended to continue his activities against the communists but in his new capacity as a private citizen. As would obviously be the case, the reports of this interview received considerable publicity. I should like to refer to the account of it which was given by the Canadian Press for July 30, 1952, in which Mr. Leopold indicated the intention to which I have just referred. In that interview Mr. Leopold gave with approval his estimate of the strength of the communist party in Canada as being from 8,000 to 9,000 card-carrying members. Mr. Leopold's statement reflected, of course, his own personal opinion which, it should be allowed, was based upon a considerable amount of official knowledge and experience. However, it did not necessarily coincide exactly with the official estimates; for at that time, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police special branch was engaged in one of its periodical assessments of party strength and official figures were in process of revision.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that the figure given by superintendent Leopold on that occasion is much the same as that which I understood my friend the hon. member for Macleod to state as being the number of card-carrying members in Mr. Leopold's opinion just the other day. With regard to the number of fellow travellers, the figure that the hon. member for Macleod mentioned was 50,000. That figure cannot be too far wrong because the number of votes cast for Labour-Progressive candidates in the last general election was 63,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I propose to raise a new subject. On this item we have been dealing with different matters and then perhaps returning to them. Before I proceed to deal with that subject, however, I simply want to make a few observations with regard to the subject which was discussed earlier by the hon. member for Kamloops and, following him, by the Prime Minister. In the discussion with regard to what is described as security within the civil service, I think there will be general agreement that it presents an extremely difficult problem. I think every one of us will recognize that there must be a great many cases in which the very nature of the employment is such that it is difficult to apply ordinary standards. Nevertheless, the thing which is causing great concern to some of us, as has been mentioned before, is the fact that, in answer to the demand that has been made on a number of occasions that the actual activity of working in support of the recognized communist party that is under the direction of Moscow should in some 83276-346J
Supply-Justice
way be defined, we have been told that a satisfactory definition cannot be given and that this might invade the realm of freedom of thought and freedom of speech. That being the case, it is extremely difficult for us to understand how something that cannot be defined in one case can be defined in the other.
Those cases which certainly arouse the greatest concern in my mind are the cases where a person is discharged or dismissed because of the allegation that he either is a communist or is sympathetic to communism. In the case mentioned by the Prime Minister, where it was decided not to permit the national film board to make certain films for the Department of National Defence, on security grounds, we know that it was quite1 clearly stated that the question of communism and communist sympathy was behind that concern. The difficulty here is that something that cannot be stated as a law in one case to create a penalty, according to the government, is used as a basis for denying the right to work in another case. Also we find that contrary to the procedure at Westminster there is no stated case placed before the civil servant concerned nor even a digest of the case in a great many instances. They are simply confronted with the fact that the finding has been made.
What it really amounts to is that we do not know what the law is and we do not know who the judges are. We neither know what definition applies nor do we know who apply that definition. Surely at a time that the rule of law is in itself one of the great issues dividing people between the free and the enslaved, we should seek on every possible occasion to err, if anything, on the side of the rule of law. I simply close my observations in this respect by asking once again that the government consider the possibility of at least an understandable definition of what the offence of communist activity or communist sympathy is which will deny a civil servant the right of employment, and I also support the arguments so ably presented by the hon. member for Kamloops that we should know who in fact are exercising this very great power in relation to many people who are carrying on duties which carry with them responsibilities and also a certain assurance of continuity of employment which is a little different from the ordinary type of employment that we would normally discuss.
Having made these observations on this subject, I wish to proceed to a subject which I raised before. It is one that I think is of very great importance at a time when freedom of the press and freedom of speech

Supply-J ustice
generally are so much in our minds. I am not dealing with this subject by way of proposal for amendment of the Criminal Code or otherwise. I wish to deal with the law as it applies to contempt of court proceedings and make certain suggestions which I hope the minister will take under consideration and then decide what can be done to deal with this aspect of a problem that has been presented to us by certain recent occurrences.
The proceedings in relation to what is described as contempt of court are in many respects today amongst the most unsatisfactory and unusual in Canadian jurisprudence. It is in fact a carry-over of ancient law. The power of judges to commit for contempt is an old common law practice. As far as Canada is concerned, we have simply inherited the statute law on this subject which goes back over a period of almost one thousand years of legal history. The British common law is part of the law of Canada except to the extent that it has been modified either by statutes of the parliament of Canada, provincial statutes, or both.
The fact is that there are at least seven sections set out in the index of the Criminal Code that deal with contempt of court, sections 165, 180, 607, 608, 678, 841 and 975. I am referring now of course to the numbers of sections in the code that has been the law for some time. Section 165 is the general section providing a penalty in the case of disobedience of orders of the court. That brings us to the fact that there are two distinct types of contempt of court. There is contempt of court which is in fact disobedience of some court order such as refusal to comply with a definite order of the court, the refusal of a witness to answer questions, or some similar disobedience of the orders of the court made under these various powers.
The second branch of this question relates to contempt outside of the court which is deemed to have some bearing on court proceedings. It is in this field that the great difficulty arises, and particularly with regard to contempt of court proceedings taken against publishers of newspapers, magazines or books and the writers of the material in those publications. Without in any way questioning the necessity for appropriate measures to enforce compliance with orders of the court, and above all for adequate protection of those who are appearing before the courts in criminal proceedings, I submit that the necessity for a clear definition of contempt of court has been given a new and somewhat dramatic emphasis by what has happened within the past few weeks.
I had occasion to refer not long ago to the warning issued by Sir Albert Walsh, chief

justice of Newfoundland, on May 18. That was a blanket warning to all residents of Newfoundland that any comments about a case then before the court against a man named Valdmanis might be regarded as contempt of court. I can find no precedent for a shotgun blast of that kind. The point with which I am greatly concerned is that a general warning of this kind that any reference to the proceedings then before the court might be interpreted as contempt of court may in fact throw a blanket of secrecy around the proceedings, which is wholly inconsistent with our concept of open, public and free trial.
Secret trials and star chamber procedure have for a very long time been regarded as inexcusable within this and other nations of the commonwealth, and we should be very careful that, no matter how good the intentions are, we should be on our guard to prevent anything creeping into our jurisprudence which would deny the completely free discussion, within proper bounds, of matters which are of concern to the people. An open trial means not only the presence of other people in court. It means not only the right of newspapers to inform others about what is happening in court. It means also the proper and legitimate discussion of the trial so that the public generally may know what is going on and what is happening under our legal system. It must be remembered that one of the things asserted over and over again is the statement that criminal punishment is perhaps intended not so much to visit a penalty upon the individual as to offer an example to others which will be a deterrent against a repetition of a similar crime.
There is a great deal of discussion at the moment about the very unpleasant details of hanging. Not one of us likes to contemplate that part of our legal procedure. However, we have been told for a very long time that it is not the thought of inflicting the death penalty upon a person guilty of murder that is so important in these proceedings as the warning it may offer to others of the penalty that follows murder or conduct of that kind. There must also certainly be an advantage to society in knowing the nature of things that will bring penalties; that is a natural consequence of one aspect of publicity in the press and over the radio. There is also the fact that the accused has an opportunity to have his case presented as well. If there were general objection to what took place then, while it might perhaps not be possible to have that public sentiment produce any satisfactory results immediately in relation to that individual, it is possible that this

expression of public sentiment will subsequently be interpreted in new laws which will follow the general development of advancement and improvement in our society.
Someone may ask why we should be so concerned about that here. This is the place, Mr. Chairman, where these things should be considered because the judges are simply called upon to interpret the laws that are passed here, in the provincial legislatures or, in their own local sphere of responsibility, by municipal councils. It is our responsibility particularly to correct anything that, by public evidence, is found to be unsatisfactory. I believe it is important that we have before us another recent case which brings this whole situation into clear focus where, in effect, a penalty was imposed as a result of what was stated to be contempt of court. I refer to the contempt of court proceedings in the Balcombe case, recently tried in Cornwall by the chief justice of Ontario, Chief Justice McRuer.
On that occasion the chief justice brought before the court certain people responsible for the sale and distribution of magazines that had referred in advance to the circumstances connected with this trial. As will be recalled, one man against whom the penalty was imposed, amongst others, was a man named Bryan. Following that the chief justice reviewed the case and changed the penalty that had been imposed. A question was raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert, and the Minister of Justice obtained a statement from Chief Justice McRuer which was placed on the record. This statement was in the third person, and appears at page 2621 of Hansard for March 3, 1954. I quote what the chief justice had to say concerning the power under which he acted in this particular case and also the power under which he reviewed the case and changed the penalty.
The matter was brought before the court by an application made by Mr. Kelly, the counsel for the accused Balcombe in the case of Regina v. Balcombe, and the material upon which the order was based was placed before Chief Justice McRuer on this application. The chief justice, exercising the inherent power vested in a judge of a court of superior jurisdiction, directed that the publishers and the distributor in the Cornwall area should be brought before the court to show cause why they should not be committed for contempt of court. In imposing the penalty.
