Chief Justice McRuer exercised the inherent power vested in a judge of any court of superior jurisdiction in a matter of this character, and likewise the chief justice in remitting part of Mr. Bryan's sentence, exercised an inherent power that is vested in a judge who imposes such a sentence when he considers that the service of part of the sentence may have sufficiently purged the contempt of the prisoner.
Supply-Justice
In that case the chief justice was simply saying this: As a judge, I have acted under the inherent power conferred upon a judge of the superior court. It is for me to decide what will constitute contempt, and it is for me to decide the penalty. Also inherent within my power as a judge of the superior court is the right to review and to decide that the penalty should be changed if that should be my opinion. It seems to me that this statement by the chief justice, to which I take no exception as an accurate interpretation of the situation as it stands, does emphasize the very loose and undefined position of publishers and others who may be called upon to distribute publications throughout Canada, and the danger in which any publisher may be under such a broad warning as that now given by the chief justice of Newfoundland.
It seems to me that these two statements brought together emphasize as never before the need for a definition of contempt of court outside of the court, and particularly contempt of court such as would constitute grounds for proceedings against a publisher or someone distributing the publication. Since the contempt of court proceedings in the Balcombe case were in regard to publications from the United States, which had been distributed and sold here, that emphasizes the fact that publishers of periodicals or newspapers in Canada with a wide circulation may be responsible in any provincial jurisdiction for what may happen there, according to the interpretation placed upon the meaning of contempt of court by any judge of a superior court of any of the provinces. Surely, that is too vague and uncertain a position when we speak with pride of the freedom of the press. It is not only the right of the press to speak with freedom about their opinions. Surely there can be no case where freedom of the press can be more important in its ultimate effect than the proper discussion of proceedings in court, where the subsequent security of the individual may depend upon the extent of the information conveyed through the press, which will bring the necessary reforms-if reforms should take place.
The law on this subject has a long history -a history going back to antiquity. In recent years however the statement in one case has been quoted over and over again with satisfaction by judges who have dealt with this matter in jurisdictions where there is an appropriate appeal.
In Great Britain the case which has been quoted most frequently, and with satisfaction, by other judges in other cases since that time, is that of Regina v. Payne and Cooper

Supply-Justice
(1896), 1 Queen's Bench, at page 557. In this report we find the following statement:
The applicant must show that something has been published which either is clearly intended, or at least is calculated, to prejudice a trial which is pending.
Mr. Chairman, if that were the test of contempt of court as it related to a statement published in the press, then there have been cases here in Canada where a penalty for contempt of court has been imposed in which it could not, in fact, have been imposed under this interpretation. It will be found that the statement in Regina v. Payne and Cooper was quoted with satisfaction in one of the leading cases on this subject in 1936 by Mr. Justice Du Parcq in the case of ex parte Gaskell and Chambers Limited (1936), 2 King's Bench, at page 595. At that time ithe subject under discussion was the very question that was raised in Newfoundland as to the publication of civil proceedings at a time when criminal proceedings are under way.
In that case the quotation I have just given from Regina v. Payne and Cooper was quoted with satisfaction, and a motion to commit was dismissed on the ground that the applicant did not show these requirements.
I mention that for this reason, that it has almost come to be taken as a definition of the condition that must be met, if an applicant is to succeed in seeking to have a penalty imposed for the publication of something in connection with a pending trial.
I know that there is under consideration at the present time a provision for an appeal in contempt cases. This is contained in the proposed amendment to the Criminal Code. I would point out however that this relates only to the right of appeal, and not to a definition.
When I raised this matter a few days ago the Minister of Justice spoke of the fact that this is something of primary concern to the provinces-to the provincial governments and legislatures-because of the exclusive provincial jurisdiction over the administration of justice. I submit that this is something definitely under the jurisdiction of this parliament, because what has come down to us as an inherent right of the courts is something clearly in the nature of criminal proceedings, because it is declared to be an offence by a judge, and a penalty is imposed.
I submit that the fact that contempt of court is within the jurisdiction of this parliament is demonstrated beyond question by the fact that we now have seven sections of the Criminal Code specifically declaring
IMr. Drew.]
certain cases where conduct of a particular kind will be held to be contempt; and a penalty is provided. If it was appropriate for this parliament to create penalties for refusal to do certain things within the courts, where the administration of justice is under provincial jurisdiction, then surely it is equally appropriate to define this type of contempt of court where there is an offence and where a penalty is imposed.
May I point out that there are a number of cases where the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in a particular field has not been accepted as a reason for not dealing with it by the parliament of Canada, where there has been something of a criminal or quasicriminal nature which called for the imposition of a penalty of such a nature as would apply to a criminal offence. And, just to give one example, I would refer to those sections in the existing Criminal Code dealing with unlawful acts in restraint of trade. Those are sections 498, 498A and 499. Surely in the ordinary course of events trade would come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments and legislatures under property and civil rights. The fact, however, that a penalty has to be imposed for certain acts that are to be described as offences was regarded as sufficient ground for dealing with that matter under the sections to which I have referred. And there are other statutory provisions which follow the same course.
It must be remembered that no suggestion of any allegation of impropriety against any judge is contained in a discussion of this subject and in the argument that the present proceedings are unsatisfactory and that any statement by any judge may in itself constitute a possible limitation of freedom of the press or freedom of the individual. We should remember at all times that our responsibility is to pass laws, and that the responsibility of the judges is to interpret those laws and to impose penalties.
The actual procedure of those courts is defined by provincial laws which state how courts will be carried on. The judges within those laws that describe the administration of justice, and under the many statutes of this parliament, of the provincial legislatures, and of the municipal councils in their local fields, must observe those laws and give evenhanded justice in relation to those who may be brought before them in connection with any of those laws. It is our responsibility and not the responsibility of the judge to make new laws. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the combination of these two statements which I have quoted and the numerous discussions in recent months and years do point out to us that the judges in these cases are called

upon to make the law, and they are also called upon to decide what the penalty will be. I submit the time is overdue for us to make the law with regard to contempt of court by publications in the press or in periodicals and even to decide what the penalty will be.
I am sure that the judges of this country, for whom by tradition and experience I have the utmost respect, would themselves welcome such a guide and such assistance in the interpretation of this extremely difficult subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understood my hon. friend to quote with approval what he describes as almost a definition of the conditions which must be met before a judge is warranted in citing for contempt. Would he not agree that what he has quoted is good law in itself? If so, wherein does the necessity of our passing a law to confirm or clarify it lie.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is exactly the situation: that does not bind our judges now. Chief Justice McRuer said he acted on the inherent authority of the judges. I could, but I do not need to, recite cases. The Minister of Justice knows of a case which has gone far beyond the limitation of this kind; what is more, the Minister of Justice knows very well that we have no appeal procedure in this country which brings cases before the courts in the way that they are brought before the courts of appeal in Britain. It was in such a case that this judgment was given. Mr. Chairman, what I am pointing out is that there is a procedure there, but it is also a procedure that is based upon long-standing judgments. We have seen fit to define contempt of court in a number of cases. If it was wise for us to define acts in those cases, I submit it is proper for us to define acts in this case. I submit in fact it is more appropriate to define contempt when it is something that relates to the freedom of the press and to the very great difficulty there must be in the minds of publishers at this time as to what actually does constitute contempt of court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Can my hon. friend tell me of the cases in which we have defined contempt of court?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is exactly the point. There is no definition at the present time. There was no attempt specifically to define what contempt is in the case to which I have referred that was dealt with by the chief justice of Ontario. It was simply his decision, under his inherent powers, that there had been contempt of court; then, it was his decision, under his inherent powers, that he had gone too far; that he subsequently
Supply-Justice
thought that a more moderate sentence would be more in keeping with the offence with which he had dealt.
There was a case here in the city of Ottawa -I think it was just three years ago-when a very reputable publication, the Ottawa Journal, was fined $3,000 for contempt of court. Without questioning the authority of the judge to impose it-I might add it was the same judge who imposed the penalty in Cornwall this year-the Journal editorially subsequently pointed out that they were puzzled as to how the court had arrived at this figure, or how the chief justice had arrived at this figure, and I should imagine everybody would be puzzled. I do not think we should be puzzled at how a judge or court arrives at penalties. I think we should know in advance what the penalties are. That does not mean we should know the exact amount. In regard to incarceration, it should not be less than a certain period and not more than a certain period, and in the case of a money penalty, it should not be less than a certain amount and not more than a certain amount. It does seem to me that it is a most extraordinarily open-ended power in the hands of any judge, no matter how much we may respect our judiciary, to leave him completely free to decide what the penalty would be. The fact is, I know nothing at the moment that would say that a penalty of a million dollars would not be within the competence of a judge if he decided that was the proper penalty to impose against some large publishing house. I know of nothing at all that suggests any uniform pattern. It is entirely at the whim of the judge himself. I am sure that all of our judges would exercise their best judgment; but, Mr. Chairman, there is another strange aspect about this. We are very much inclined to make sure that in most cases the persons who feel themselves offended will not themselves judge what should be done. That is because we recognize we are all human beings, even judges.
In this case it is perfectly true that the offence technically is an offence against the court. Nevertheless, in a number of cases that have come forward recently, and I would refer particularly to one which was decided in Vancouver within the last few weeks, it was obvious that there was some feeling that this is an allegation against the judge and the jurors as individuals. Nevertheless, the judge who saw himself affected by what had been alleged or stated was himself the one who created the law and said what the contempt was in this case. Without in any way seeking to review the decision, I may say that it was a very unusual type of contempt, to say the least. Then, also the same judge,

Supply-Justice
having declared the law in that particular case, and a very unusual law it was, he imposed the penalty. I do not think that is in keeping with our ordinary practice. Surely our practice is not only to define an offence, to define a penalty, but also to allow a thing of this kind to be dealt with in an atmosphere of objective detachment, which may be very difficult for even the most high-minded individual when that individual himself may feel that there has been some reflection on him personally, as there appears to be in the case in Vancouver to which I have referred.
This suggests to me a further reason why it is vitally important that we should provide safeguards against injustice. When I use the word "injustice" I am applying that neither to any judge nor to anyone who has dealt with any of these cases. I apply it to injustice within the law. I point out, however, that this is the high court of parliament. This is the place to decide now whether the time has come to follow the same practice as has been followed in cases that perhaps could have much less serious consequences in their general impact upon society, and to define both the offence and the penalty and to make sure that the person who deals with the question will, in the ordinary course of events, most likely not be the person who has himself been affected. I should also like to point out another matter related to the statement by Sir Albert Walsh, chief justice of Newfoundland, in relation to the warning given to the public of Newfoundland with reference to these recent decisions which have been made which affected publishers in other cases.
I know there have been cases in Britain where under the most severe limitation publication of civil proceedings has been described as contempt of court. That was only, however, where it was done in a way that was likely to prejudice the individual, and that was very carefully pointed out in the case I cited where the application was refused on that very ground.
I would point out that in this case in Newfoundland, without in any way going into the merits, the allegation in a civil case is precisely the same as in a criminal case so there should be no possibility of prejudice to the individual concerned by a repetition in a much simpler form of the very allegation repeated over and over again in connection with criminal proceedings.
I remember distinctly how well established a practice it is to publish civil proceedings. As the Minister of Justice knows, I was for some time master of the supreme court of Ontario, and I remember that one of the

regular proceedings each day was for the press to come and obtain copies of civil proceedings that had been heard in master's chambers.
These were published with complete freedom and there was never the slightest chance that any single detail in any of these civil proceedings could possibly be subject to restraint unless an order had been made declaring that they should not be published.
I place this before the Minister of Justice, Mr. Chairman, that if there is to be any restraint on publication of this kind in regard to civil proceedings it should only be under order. After all, that is a simple procedure.
I recall very well a case that the Minister of Justice will probably remember, namely, the famous Miller will case. Many people are not aware that one very interesting paragraph in that will has never been published. It is a most unusual paragraph and it was not published because it would have caused considerable embarrassment to certain individuals and dependents. The order was obtained on proper application supported by convincing evidence that it would cause embarrassment, and that there was no real necessity for its publication. Under that order that paragraph has never been published to this day, interesting though the will was and still is.
I can recall other orders where, because of indecency or slanderous statements and things of that kind, orders were made in very rare cases in regard to particular paragraphs of some documents. That, I submit, Mr. Chairman, is the proper procedure. In that case the court knows, the public knows, and everyone has a right to know what may or may not be published.
I think it is contrary to our whole idea of free and open trial before the courts to place blanket warnings before the public which might carry forward this very uncertain, unsatisfactory and unsound practice, in regard to contempt of court proceedings in relation to the press, a stage still further in connection with the proceedings now under way.
In my opinion this threat to newspapers in Newfoundland indicates that this whole question of contempt of court has got completely out of hand. It should not be necessary for me to repeat, as I did once before, that personally I have the highest regard for Sir Albert Walsh in his judicial and personal capacity, as I have for every member of that bench.
But it is my responsibility, as it is the responsibility of every member of this high court of parliament, to deal with any matter

that comes before us where we think a possible injustice may be done or something be done affecting the general welfare of our society.
It is in that light that I have brought this matter before the Minister of Justice today, and I would point out that the chief justice of Newfoundland expressed some concern about the trial of this case by press and radio.
I do not take exception to certain statements in regard to the rights of the individual that were made, but I would point out that it was also by press and radio that the chief justice issued his warning which, with an undefined law, may have a very limiting effect upon freedom of the press and freedom of speech in that part of Canada which has a longer tradition, in many respects, of judicial proceedings than other parts of Canada with which Newfoundland is now joined as part of one nation.
I would also point out that the proceedings which took place in Newfoundland are likely to have their effect upon the proceedings that take place in other parts of Canada.
The question arises as to what parliament can do. I submit that, entirely contrary to what the Minister of Justice said the other day about the administration of justice bringing this within the jurisdiction of the provinces, this is a subject under the authority of parliament. It has been so declared in other cases of contempt. There is an offence and there is a penalty. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is entirely in keeping with the other section now in the code, and other sections in other laws, that we should be prepared to deal with this subject.
I believe the Minister of Justice could very well have legislation framed during the course of the present session. After all, there is certain legislation not yet before us. It Would be possible to define this law in a very simple way and, Mr. Chairman, I for one would feel much more satisfied about the situation if there were a clear definition which made it quite certain that the likelihood of injury to someone being tried must definitely and unquestionably be proved, and also that there be some definite limits both to the penalty that may be imposed by way of jail sentence, and to the penalty that may be imposed by way of a fine.
This, Mr. Chairman, is something that has been discussed quite often, and I know it has been before the Minister of Justice to an extent. But I submit there would still be time to draft a satisfactory statute dealing with this subject, and I believe the freedom of the press and the right of the press to the time-honoured protection of knowing what the law is in advance demands that
Supply-Justice
this high court of parliament define this particular type of contempt, as other types have been defined, and take away from the judges for their own satisfaction as well as ours what members of this high court of parliament have, namely the responsibility for deciding the extent of the penalty that can be imposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the same manner as the Leader of the Opposition, I have a very high regard for Sir Albert Walsh and his colleagues on the Newfoundland bench, and likewise for Chief Justice McRuer and his colleagues of the supreme court of Ontario. I think that my hon. friend would agree with me that we can share an equally high opinion of the judges in the Canadian courts generally.
Is this therefore not the situation? For many long years-for decades if not for generations-the parliament of Great Britain and the parliament and the legislatures of Canada also, having a high opinion of judges, have not felt that they were under the necessity of defining what constituted contempt of court or of setting the limits of the penalties that could be imposed for it. If the need for that which my hon. friend is now requesting be an inherent one, if it be something in the nature of things, as he seems to represent it, I should think the likelihood is that it would have made itself felt some time before now.
There are one or two distinctions to be drawn here. For example, when my hon. friend raised this matter the other day, he was speaking not about contempt of court but about a warning which had been given by Chief Justice Sir Albert Walsh and his colleagues of the superior court of Newfoundland in the city of St. John's, arising out of the publication by the newspapers there of some material. My suggestion to my hon. friend was that, if he were, as I understood him to be, objecting to that warning as an improper act in the administration of justice, it was a matter which was the concern of the attorney general of Newfoundland because that matter is clearly involved in the administration of justice in Newfoundland. If that warning were to be followed in the actual trial itself by citation by Sir Albert or any of his colleagues of anyone for disregarding the warning or in some other way committing a contempt of court, I do not share my hon. friend's view that the presiding judge in a trial, in the exercise of the inherent right of the court to punish for contempt in order that it may have that proper control over its own trials that it should have if it is to conduct them properly,

Supply-Justice
can do this capriciously or, to use my hon. friend's word, at the presiding judge's whim. He cannot introduce some new concept of contempt of court and, on the basis of this concept in his own mind, cite for contempt and impose a penalty.
For my hon. friend himself quoted-and I thought very aptly indeed-one of the leading cases in England which said that, in order to prove contempt of court, the applicant must show that something has been published that was clearly intended or at least was calculated to mislead a trial which was pending. I think it is a fairly elementary proposition that if the judge in any court wishes properly, in accordance with the decided cases as to what contempt of court is, to cite for contempt of court, he must act in accordance with the jurisprudence which has been built up upon the subject of contempt of court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the Minister of Justice but I would point out that in the Vancouver case that was not the test. It was something entirely different. It was after a verdict had actually been given.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I really hesitate to discuss the Vancouver case, the Bal-combe case or these other cases, and for this amongst other reasons. In terms of the definition that my hon. friend quoted, and with which offhand I venture to agree-I think this is a very good statement of the jurisprudence upon the subject of this particular kind of contempt of court-my hon. friend will see by the most casual perusal of the definition he cited that the applicant must show that something has been published which clearly is intended or at least is calculated to mislead the trial which is pending. That, Mr. Chairman, is a question of fact. One of the greatest difficulties we have in discussing the merits of the contempt of court in the Balcombe case or the possible contempt of court in the case in Newfoundland or the merits of the warning that was issued in Newfoundland as applied to the facts there-one reason why it is almost impossible to discuss these things intelligently is that they hinge upon the facts, and we do not have a comprehensive statement of the facts.
This is an extremely important matter, and it is very much to the credit of the Leader of the Opposition that he raised it. After he brought it up the other day I wrote to Sir Albert Walsh the following letter dated May 31:
Dear Sir Albert:
I am enclosing herewith the Hansard report of May 27, 1954, in which is recorded an exchange between the Leader of the Opposition and myself with regard to a statement attributed to you in the Daily News of St. John's.

One of the difficulties of discussing a question of this sort intelligently in the House of Commons is that, in a matter which it seems to me hinges largely upon fact, we do not have a comprehensive statement of the facts. If, therefore, you could directly or if you think it preferable, through the Attorney General of Newfoundland, put me in possession of material relevant to any discussion which may be opened up by the Leader of the Opposition or others, such a course would, I think, lessen the possibility of the debates here creating a misunderstanding by Canadian public opinion of the issues involved.
That is one reason why it is so difficult to deal with, as finally and as conclusively as they deserve to be dealt with, the points raised by my friend the Leader of the Opposition.
However, in general terms I think this much can be said. To begin with, with great deference, in the light of the case law which my hon. friend himself cited, which is fairly clear and explicit of one type of contempt, I would doubt as to whether there is any definition which we could insert in the Criminal Code or in any other statute which would be any clearer or better statement of what that type of contempt consisted, than what my hon. friend referred to- and very correctly-as almost a definition of the conditions which must be met before the judge is entitled to cite for contempt of court. On that point therefore I would doubt very much whether it was desirable that we should insert a section to that effect in the Criminal Code, something which, as my hon. friend himself has proven, is already dealt with in the jurisprudence upon the subject. If we did so-as I am sure he would be the first to agree-we could only do so in relation to those criminal courts which are referred to in the Criminal Code itself. Rather than do that, the royal commission which was charged with the task of consolidating the code, our own Department of Justice and, up until the present time, the House of Commons and the other place- although I understand that the members of the other place are examining this particular provision at the present time-have thought that the substantial points which my friend the Leader of the Opposition has raised today might be properly met by providing, as the new Criminal Code consolidation bill provides in clause 9:
Where a court, judge, justice or magistrate summarily convicts a person for a contempt of court and imposes punishment in respect thereof, that person may, with leave of the court of appeal or a judge thereof, appeal to the court of appeal
(a)	from the conviction, or
(b)	against the punishment imposed.
It continues in subsection 2 as follows:
For the purposes of an appeal under subsection (1) the provisions of Part XVIII apply, mutatis mutandis.

That means, as I am sure my hon. friend will agree, that for the first time in Canada we will have an appeal both from the conviction and the sentence in respect of a citation for contempt of court. This appeal will enable the appeal court to deal with the question of what constitutes contempt of court, or to use my hon. friend's term, what is its proper definition. Thus it will cover the case in which a judge, purporting to cite for contempt of court, has imposed a penalty for something which, whatever it may be, is not contempt of court. All these points can go before the court of appeal; and there can also go before the court of appeal for reconsideration the adequacy of the sentence which has been imposed. Thus I would think, with great deference, that in the new Criminal Code Bill No. 7 we have anticipated my hon. friend and have gone already as far as we should go in this direction which he has suggested.
With regard to contempt of court committed in a civil court, without going into the matter too carefully I would be inclined to think that an appeal from a citation for contempt of court occurring in provincial courts exercising civil jurisdiction would more than likely have to be provided by provincial legislation. For offhand I cannot entirely accept my hon. friend's suggestion that contempt of court is a crime in the narrow sense. I would say that the power to cite for contempt of court is an inherent power of a court of superior jurisdiction to control the proceedings before the court itself, and that if there are to be any limitations upon the power to cite for contempt in a provincial court of civil jurisdiction dealing with civil cases the question would have to be carefully looked into as to whether that could be provided by any other than provincial legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I want to deal very briefly with two points raised by the Minister of Justice. First of all, I am very strongly of the opinion that this is properly a subject for action by parliament. I would point out that section 164 of the existing code indicates how far parliament has gone in dealing with penalties relating to matters that may come under not only laws of the parliament of Canada but provincial laws as well. The minister will remember that section 164 reads as follows:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment who, without lawful excuse, disobeys any act of the parliament of Canada or of any legislature in Canada by wilfully doing any act which it forbids, or omitting to do any act which it requires to be done, unless some penalty or other mode of punishment is expressly provided by law.
Supply-Justice
I read that for this reason. This is intended to make sure that there shall be no loose interpretation of the inherent authority of the court but rather that in any case where any act, either of the parliament of Canada or of a provincial legislature, calls for something to be done, the failure to carry out that obligation renders the person liable to one year's imprisonment for such failure if some penalty has not otherwise been provided either by the parliament of Canada, under its jurisdiction with relation to criminal law because otherwise it would have no right to enter that field, or by the provincial legislature. I mention that because I submit, while it is not on all fours with the problem before us, that it does indicate the extent to which, under the general authority of the parliament of Canada, anything that savours of criminal Jaw or a criminal offence or punitive action is within our jurisdiction and calls for action.
With respect to the point made by the Minister of Justice about the quotation I gave from the case I described as the leading case at the moment in Britain, I would point out that does not apply here because the judges here act under the inherent power of the court, as Chief Justice McRuer said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They do in England too.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Oh yes, but of course, as the Minister of Justice knows, there is an appeal procedure which over the years has established very clearly a definite jurisprudence. That is exactly the point I am making. These cases to which I refer are cases that follow a definite line of precedents. I have pointed out in support of my contention that we need something here to define the penalty in line with other definitions and stated penalties. The fact is that we have had cases in Canada which have clearly demonstrated that our judges do not feel themselves bound by the limitation to which I have already referred in regard to publication of matter in the press.
It is with that thought in mind that I submit that if offences in court against the orders of the court need to be defined it is even more necessary, in relation to those things that go out to hundreds, thousands and millions of people for reading, that the offence should be defined and the definition should be in the simplest, most understandable form. Without suggesting that it should be limited to that, I certainly would feel very much more satisfied if a simple statute were enacted that merely interpreted in statute form the definition I quoted from the English case and also what the maximum penalty will be.

Supply-Justice
I can only repeat that as the situation stands at the moment some publication which might be assessed a penalty of $1 million- and in these days of high penalties that is not an impossibility-would have no argument to sustain the claim that that was an excessive penalty. Surely with the best of judges and with the best of intent on the part of these judges, which no one questions, it is not consistent with our practice to leave such wide powers in the hands of any judge at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I should like to make two observations. First we were under the impression that by providing an appeal we were meeting the very points which my hon. friend has just now so clearly enunciated. The other point is this. Does my hon. friend really think that we would be well advised to use our power to enact statutes in relation to the criminal law to attempt to define what should be contempt of court and the punishment therefore in civil actions in the provincial courts of civil jurisdiction? Should such statutes not be left to the provincial legislatures to enact even if we had the power to enact them?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I submit that the action under which a person is haled before a court by way of contempt of court proceedings is in fact a criminal proceeding and that it should be dealt with in that way for the whole of Canada so that in every part of the country publishers will know exactly what they have a right to do and will be warned in advance, in accordance with our ordinary concept of justice, of the things that they must not do.
Mr. Chairman, if the discussion on this phase is over, there is one matter I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would not object if I were to interrupt him at this moment to ask the hon. member for Prince Albert if he wishes to follow the same line of discussion as the Leader of the Opposition. If the hon. member for Vancouver East is agreeable, I think we might make our debate more orderly if we followed the same line of argument.
Could I say a word on this point?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Vancouver East agreeable that the hon. member should follow the same line of discussion?
I presume I can follow after this subject is finished.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Yes. I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member.
I presume I can follow afterwards?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but I thought we might make our discussion more orderly by discussing one subject at a time.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of attempting to give my view as to what should be done about the law of contempt or of stepping in between the Leader of the Opposition and the Minister of Justice. However, I believe something should be cleared up in connection with this matter. The Leader of the Opposition expressed his respect for the Newfoundland bench and the chief justice of Newfoundland. He did say something else in connection with the Valdmanis case that should be mentioned because people do read the spicy parts of speeches.
In referring to the Valdmanis case the Leader of the Opposition mentioned secret trials and star chamber proceedings. I do not think the Leader of the Opposition would like that phrase to stand in connection with this matter because he knows, and everybody in this house knows, that there are no secret trials or star chamber proceedings in Newfoundland.

There is one matter I should like to mention on this item because it is a policy matter, and I do not know of any other item in the estimates under which it could be raised. Actually, it is a request to the Minister of Justice to use his position in a way I think will prove of benefit to Canada as a whole.
Unfortunately, there are those people who, for one reason or another, come into conflict with the law. When they are caught, they have to pay the penalty of the law. In these modern days of penology the old punitive idea is rapidly disappearing, and I am certain that all of us in this house are very pleased that this forward step has been made in the penitentiary system in Canada. I personally know of the progress being made and I want to add my words of commendation concerning the changes that have taken place in recent years. The minister is most certainly to be congratulated on that phase of the activities of his department.
I am certain the minister will agree with the idea that once a person comes out of the penitentiary after serving the penalty for his crime against society, it is the hope of everyone in authority that the person can take his place as a respected and responsible member of society. I feel I am absolutely safe in saying that in the majority of cases the various police authorities do not obstruct those

who have served the penalty and who try to become useful members of society. I know a great many of the members of the various police forces of Canada who do everything they possibly can to co-operate and to help those who have served a term in prison. I want to emphasize that statement I have just made, that in my opinion the majority of the officers of the police forces go out of their way to assist because of what I am now going to say.
It is unfortunate, but there is a minority in the police forces of Canada, and I include the R.C.M.P., who do not take the position that these people who break the law and have served their penalty should be assisted. I am not speaking from hearsay or rumour. I am speaking from a working knowledge of the fact that unfortunately there are a few on the police forces, including the R.C.M.P., who will go out of their way to persecute a person who has served a sentence, instead of helping him. I ask the Minister of Justice, as the nominal head of law and justice in this country, as well as the R.C.M.P., if there is any way of issuing a directive to indicate that these people should be helped if they are deserving of help.
I could take a great deal of time in giving instance after instance to prove my point, but I am just going to give one. I am not going to mention any names because that would not be fair, and it would only give publicity to the matter. I definitely know of a man who broke the law-no question about it. He was found guilty and paid the penalty. He spent a term in the penitentiary, and I was convinced he had learned his lesson. He came out determined he would never go back. He got himself a job and proved he had ability. He rose to be manager of the company. He had a family, and then what happened? No sooner had he become established than the R.C.M.P. came in and told his employer he had a record. Fortunately for this man he was wise, and had told his employer when he applied. He was staying at a motel, and the R.C.M.P. officer went to the motel owner and told him the man had a record and to get rid of him.
This went on for a period of time, and at last the man could not stand any more of it. He moved about two provinces away and got another job. He proved himself again and rose to be the top salesman for this company so that now he is the boss over all the other salesmen. His life, Mr. Chairman, is still being made a living hell on his route. Many of the customers upon whom he calls are told, even before he gets there, that this man is going to travel that route. During the last two months, because of the weather in the prairie provinces, he tried to
Supply-Justice
avoid that embarrassment by going into British Columbia. In the city of Kamloops, what happened? He was there one day when the R.C.M.P. came into the hotel and he was driven out again. As I say, I am not mentioning any names. I am just citing one case, and I am glad it is rare. You can see what that could do to a man who is trying to make good, and who has paid the penalty.
I shall be glad, in confidence, to turn the entire information over to my hon. friend. I am going to reiterate what I said before, that in the majority of cases the police officers are found to be co-operative. There are some who take this attitude of persecution. I hope the minister can perhaps do something, either directly or through some other medium, to make it clear to all law enforcement officers that they should be very careful in protecting people, and very careful in watching those they think are not going to reform. However, when they see a man or woman trying to rehabilitate themselves, trying to be good citizens, the officers should help them instead of trying to drive them down.
There is one other case I would like to refer to the minister, in the hope that perhaps he can do something about it. It is a case which I had brought to my attention about two years ago, and concerns a young man who was called from his home by his chum. They were going down the street, and the chum-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member for a moment, to say only this, that what my hon. friend states in relation to this case is so completely at variance with the instruction and the traditions of the mounted police that I know he will not take offence if I say I find it extremely difficult to believe. But I will welcome his bringing all the details of the case before me; and he may rest completely assured that it will have the most careful investigation. And if there is any foundation for the allegations which my hon. friend has made, he may be sure the proper steps will be taken.

I welcome the remarks of the minister. That is one of the reasons I mentioned it, because I was certain he would get up and make a definite statement. And may I suggest that I am not speaking of one case, or a particular record. I am speaking from experience in a number of cases. I reiterate that this is not to be taken as a criticism of the majority of law enforcement officers in this dominion, or of the R.C.M.P. But I wish to get across the point that there is still a minority who are not doing what the minister wants. I said a moment ago

Supply-Justice
that I will be glad to turn over the complete file of this particular case, in confidence. That is one sample. I could give him quite a number.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be glad to have them all.

And then, on the other point- and to me it is the important point. From my understanding it can be handled only by the federal government, or perhaps by the house. It refers to a young man in his teens who, along with his chum, was out on the street. Apparently this chum was not too good, and told this boy that he wanted to go behind a store for a few minutes. While the chum did not know it the other boy was breaking and entering. They were arrested. The boy who broke and entered was sentenced, and the other boy was let go on a suspended sentence. He never spent a day in a provincial jail, or a day in a penitentiary -and never has in his whole life.
Some time later he got a job. Just to indicate his ability, let me say that he worked up to a position where he had to be bonded. An application was made by the company-one of the best known companies in Canada-for the bond. They received a refusal-"his name is on a police blotter". He lost his job.
Then he got another job, and five years later had worked up to an administrative position, where he had to be bonded. Again the company gave the answer: "No, his name is on a police blotter". Sir, today that man has lost all hope; he is frustrated; he is an itinerant worker; his wife and child have left him-all because the bonding company will not give him a bond, all because twenty-three years ago his name was put on a police blotter, under the circumstances I have described. And even after that period of time, the bonding company will not give him a bond.
I took the matter up with the local police department and asked if something could be done. The answer was: "We are sorry. We agree with you. We know this man. We know his father-he was an officer of this police force. But we cannot do a thing about it; it is the law. It is something that comes under the federal government."
I have not been able to find out how the matter stands, and what can be done about it. And that is the first of three such cases that have come to my attention. I thought I would raise the matter here and ask the minister if there is anything that can be done, or is required to be done, so far as the law is concerned, in a case of that kind.
TMr. Wincii.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I understood my hon. friend correctly it would seem to me that this has not anything to do with the police. It has only to do with the policy of the bonding company. That company, controlling its own money and its own business policy, is entitled to say upon what terms it will grant a bond. If the company has a fixed policy that will not grant a bond to anyone who has a criminal record, however slight or however long ago, then that company policy would prevent the issuance of a bond. The police were quite correct when they told my hon. friend that there was nothing they could do about it. But they were not correct if, as he said, they told him that that was the law.
There is no law about it at all. If he was convicted and was released on suspended sentence, he was in fact convicted. That fact is recorded in a public record. And if the bonding company will not issue a bond, that is not the fault of the police or the law. I doubt very much if we could pass a law here, other than one which would expunge convictions from the records beyond a certain date, which would change the situation of which my hon. friend complains.

Mr. Chairman, I would refer first to the statement made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I must say that when he stated that even a minority of the R.C.M.P. were hounding persons within this country who at some time had been convicted, it is something that is not in keeping with my experience nor, I am sure, the experience of Canadians generally.
The mounted police need no defence. For many years, to a degree experienced by perhaps only a few in the house, I have appeared opposite them, and I have never known this distinguished body, either in a minority or in a majority, to do anything that would interfere with the rehabilitation of any person who at any time had committed an offence.
The R.C.M.P. need no defence; and I think the hon. gentleman would have been far better advised had he placed this case before the authorities. If, as he says, there are several cases, then I think the minister should ask for those several cases, because apparently there is a concentration in one province of such wrongdoing that is not to be found in the other provinces.
I say this because I feel that to generalize, as the hon. member has done, in regard to this great force, with its traditions for service, for honour and for proper police protection, and to castigate them even as a minority

before the House of Commons, does not give to them that degree of fairness that I feel they deserve.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kamloops is to be congratulated on the effective manner in which he discussed this very serious problem of preserving and maintaining the security of the state while, at the same time, maintaining the rights of the individual to the maximum extent. This afternoon parliament discussed a subject worthy of the best traditions of the House of Commons.
Generally speaking, it is good that from time to time major questions such as this should be considered with the fullest and frankest exchange of opinions. We realize the danger which we face nationally and internationally from communism. However, in meeting communism, we must not allow ourselves to drift into a condition that might be described as a garrison state. In meeting the terrible challenge that communism has raised as against freedom everywhere in the world the major responsibility of democratic parliaments today is to endeavour at all times not to imperil unnecessarily personal rights and freedom beyond that boundary wherein the safety of the state must be of paramount importance and must be maintained.
This afternoon the Prime Minister dealt with this matter at considerable length. At times I felt he was having difficulty in explaining his support for a system which has its imperfections, which had its shortcomings and its dangers revealed by the hon. member for Kamloops and which inherently in its constitution is a denial of the rule of law and the maintenance of the rights of the individual. Everywhere, among nations with a democratic background and a parliamentary heritage, the same difficulty besets the endeavours of governments to achieve their purposes through established institutions.
The hon. member for Kamloops showed what had been done in Britain. I intend to refer to what is being done or projected in the United States to the end that, where there are in the present system shortcomings that endanger the rights of the individual, those rights shall be maintained within the widest possible limits consistent with safety.
Supply-Justice
Parliament today found out for the first time that the Secretary of State was the chairman of this committee during a period of time. Because of the knowledge he possesses, the Secretary of State is one who should at least give the committee some idea of the operation of this secret committee. History shows that anonymously-manned committees dealing with the freedom of the individual are generally the prelude to the denial of the rights of the individual. Such procedure is the antithesis of freedom. It subjects the individual not to the rule of law but to the arbitrarily capricious exercise of the power of the state. These things are necessarily so when danger threatens. What parliament has to face is this fact. While we want to assure our security as of the first importance, under no circumstances do we want anything in the nature of a star chamber that operates behind closed doors, is presided over by the instrument of anonymity, that carries out its work without the evidence of the individual accused, and which, by the course that it follows, pronounces upon that individual, in the event of his being found unfit, a penalty that will remain with him throughout life.
Today, as always, there are those who challenge freedom. I listened to the Leader of the Opposition today dealing with some remarks made by the chief justice of Newfoundland to the press of that province, which anticipated that the press might commit an offence for which punishment was intimated.
Freedom cannot survive without hospitality to ideas with which we disagree. I fear for freedom when the right of the press to speak fearlessly and to report fairly is challenged at any time. There is that everlasting conflict between freedom of speech and the fear of it. There is an everlasting conflict between, on the one hand, the tendency to suppress what we disagree with, and on the other the right to speak as we wish, so long as in speaking we do not speak treasonably, seditiously, blasphemously or libellously. Without freedom of the press there can be no political liberty. It will soon be a memory. That is why I agree with what the hon. gentleman said, that the right of the individual to appeal against conviction registered for contempt is in the nature of a reform that has been long needed and required.
I know of no better definition of what freedom of the press means than that once spoken by Jefferson when he said:
The basis of our governments being the opinion of the people, the very first object should be to keep that right; and were it left to me to decide

Supply-Justice
whether we should have a government without newspapers or newspapers without a government, X should not hesitate a moment to prefer the latter. But I should mean that every man should receive those papers and be capable of reading them.
Freedom of the press is challenged when warnings are made in advance as to what will take place if the newspapers do what they have the right to do, namely, to report fairly and accurately the facts of a case. And the challenge is multiplied where there is no right of appeal after conviction when the newspaper does its duty and publishes what it is entitled to do.
I cannot see what the challenge to security is in having revealed the names of the members of this committee. Shall we have a body charged with the power to determine a man's reputation for all time to come? A body that is anonymous? That body may bd right in most of the conclusions it comes to, but a secret tribunal is a perversion of justice and a denial of our heritage.
I ask the minister to explain where there is in our security that which requires that this committee shall remain undesignated. Why should not the accused have the right to give evidence before that body? I realize that the identity of his accusers cannot be made available to him, otherwise it might very well be that the entire system of counter-espionage would be defeated. But surely an individual, anonymously charged, anonymously proceeded against, should have the right to know something of the general nature of the charge. Surely he has a right not to be condemned in a secret tribunal, meeting secretly, and coming to a decision behind closed doors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am quite sure my hon. friend does not wish to mislead the committee. It has been explained on a great many occasions that the secret panel, to which my hon. friend has referred, does not deal with any of these individual cases at all. It deals with the general question of security, questions of policy, and the like. But the idea that the case of a person who is suspected of being a poor security risk comes up before the security panel is quite without foundation.

I do not say that they come before the security panel. I say the security panel determines the question, and the person whose reputation will be destroyed by suspicion and by the action taken should at least have the right to answer.
But let the minister reply to me when I have concluded my remarks, because I have some suggestions to make in connection with this matter. I admit it cannot be a public

investigation, but we do not want it to be by a legislative committee either. The experience in recent weeks of a public investigation of communist wrongdoers or potential wrongdoers is a perversion of democracy where trial takes place by innuendo and where, in the public mind, conviction takes place by suspicion.
No, not by a public legislative committee. After all, in an organization such as that, headline hunting takes the place of judicial calm, and guilt is determined on the basis of the charge laid, regardless of the evidence.
It cannot be publicly done; it cannot be by public inquiry. If it is to be done in the only way available, namely through consideration by representatives on a panel, I suggest this, that first and foremost there should be the right to answer, and where therq is any preponderance of evidence the security of the state shall determine the result.
But surely the principle of an anonymous tribunal need not necessarily be adopted in order either to preserve the security of the state or to assure justice.
A recent case in the United States is of interest. That is the case of Dr. Oppenheimer who was suspended last December, and who made his appeal to the atomic energy commission security board. That board made its decision yesterday, and by a majority of two to one determined that, while Dr. Oppenheimer was not guilty of any direct offence, in the interests of security the acceptance of his withdrawal in December, as requested, should be continued.
But apparently that is not to be the final move. In yesterday's issue of the Christian Science Monitor President Eisenhower is reported to have said that the Oppenheimer case is still going through a quasi-judicial process and that until the appeal was finally settled he would not comment.
In that I think there is a suggestion that might well be adopted in this country, namely that in any decision that is made adverse to the individual he should at least have available a quasi-judicial appeal, at which he could present his side of the case so that injustice shall not be done, and so that unfairness will not be allowed to pass unchallenged, while at the same time maintaining the security of the state.
After all, this is a very difficult problem to handle. It is one that challenges the ingenuity of those who would meet it. These things admitted, nonetheless I believe this. Every individual should have the right of appeal to a quasi-judicial body, not meeting openly, in order to give him the opportunity, whoever the accused may be, to place his side

erf the case before that body to the end that, in maintaining our security, we do not go to the length of making possible the sacrifice of an innocent man's future by the failure to provide those safeguards which freedom, throughout the years, has established to maintain and assure the maintenance of the freedom of the individual.
Only the other day I came upon a novel that was written in the first world war and which, I think, epitomizes what I have been trying to place before the committee. It was one written by Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch. The title page reads as follows:
The best revenge on your enemy is not to be like him.
The story that is revealed in this novel is of two antagonists, each steeped in hatred of the other and who, after years, grew to resemble each other so closely that at the end it became hard to tell one from the other.
Mr. Chairman, let us maintain our national security in the world of today but let us not go to the point that we sacrifice the freedoms for which we contend and imitate the thing we hate in order to defeat that thing. That represents the viewpoint that I think might be brought before the committee. It is not advanced in any spirit of criticism but in a realization that, in the cold war of today that seems destined to continue for many years in our generation, first and foremost in this citadel of freedom each of us must speak out to the end that there may be preserved that degree of freedom which will assure the mainsprings of resistance against the forces of communism. I do not believe that those mainsprings can be maintained by sacrificing them unnecessarily for the expediency of the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take only a moment or two of the time of the committee to express my opinion with regard to the department run by the Minister of Justice. I think we as Canadians can all be proud of the groups of people who come under his jurisdiction, and we can all hope that they will continue to be maintained at the high standard at which they are maintained today.
I would refer particularly to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I think that every member of parliament and also a great many citizens of this country have heard the words of praise from visitors to this country with regard to their appearance, their efficiency and their integrity. I am glad to know that the present minister is maintaining that high standard in this extremely important force.
Supply-Justice
I should also like to pay him a compliment on the way in which our penal institutions under his jurisdiction have been maintained. I think we have every reason to be justly proud of the little trouble we have had in our penitentiaries in the past years. I also think that we can and should show the same admiration towards the judges of this country; and it is on this point that I wish to say the few words that I am going to say tonight.
The judges in this country have had the happy position of being well respected ever since the founding of the dominion. Anything that might happen to them to change this opinion of the people would be a serious detriment to the country. Since the end of the war there have been numerous cases where our judiciary have been used to arbitrate in industrial disputes. It may be extremely flattering to the judiciary to be picked as arbitrators on these boards, but I do not believe that this is a good way for the judges of our country to be used. To me the work of a judge in administering justice seems to be a different field from that of an arbitrator. It is necessary for an arbitrator to stretch justice one way or the other so that a plane of mutual understanding can be reached. I do not like to think for a minute that justice in our courts should be regarded as something that could be stretched one way or the other in order to meet some compromising position between two opinions. I do not believe the man lives who can spend weeks and weeks in making extremely important decisions which are not justice decisions but which are expedient decisions, without an effect being produced upon his opinions. I cannot help feeling that the people who sit and watch the performance in these arbitration cases cannot have the proper respect for the arbitrator acting as a judge after they have had the experience of watching one of these arbitration cases.
I think it is highly important to this country that some method be found to relieve the judges of the responsibility of accepting positions as arbitrators. Not only do we have the two different schools of thought-they are different; and I sincerely hope they will always remain so-but we have judges absent from their offices for weeks at a time when the lawyers in that community- and I am not a lawyer-have not the access to the judge which they should have. This absenteeism must make the position of many solicitors extremely difficult. I should therefore like to see the Minister of Justice spend the time that is necessary to make with the provinces the arrangements, which must be made, to return our judges to their benches,

Supply-Justice
so that they may not be put in the position where labour leaders and management both leel that it is not justice that is being dispensed and where, in some cases, they will exhort their supporters to disregard the opinion of a man whose opinion should not be disregarded.
I would plead with the minister that he take the steps that are necessary for the discontinuance of this practice of using judges on arbitration commissions.
It may be that the judges should be paid more. I am not in a posiiton to argue one way or the other about that, but it certainly should be made perfectly clear that a condition exists now that did not exist ten years ago and it should not be allowed to continue for years. If the process of arbitration is to be permanent, if it is to go on down through the years, then it is time that we changed our system so that we will not have judges acting as arbitrators in labour disputes.

Mr. Chairman, I will be brief but I have something to say. 1 do not doubt the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I think he will get somewhere with the Minister of Justice, but his experience is not mine. I have sponsored a great many convicted people, I think about 172, released on permit or parole, and only three have failed. Even they did not fail very badly. One man was the worst because he could not keep away from liquor. My worst problem is not the police. The worst problem I meet in trying to rehabilitate some of these men is their own thinking. I have never had a boy under 20 years of age who was a repeater.
When the Prime Minister was minister of justice he said that it was in the best interests of human beings not to make them serve the full term of their sentences. Our present Solicitor General was kind enough to let me have a boy when he had only served half his sentence last week which shows that the Department of Justice and the minister have not changed their attitude. I think it is in the best interests of the man who makes a mistake not to make him serve his full term, and I think the Minister of Justice will support that statement.
We have a man in Fort William now who has been a repeater. I refused to sponsor him when he was released this time because I could not believe him. You have to judge a man by his conduct, and I am still hoping that some day he will change his mind and go to the proper source for help to overcome his difficulties. I must say that I have had co-operation from our police in Fort William. In the case of one man who was released on

permit the mounted police went further in my opinion than I thought they should go, further than I would go because I was a little bit afraid that the man would not keep his word. That prisoner came from Westminster jail and not from Fort William.
The mounted police have co-operated with me splendidly, and I think that the hon. member for Vancouver East will find that the case he mentioned will be cleared up completely either by the Minister of Justice or by the chief of the remission branch. I do not doubt his experience at all. It is heartburning to a man who is trying to make good to be hounded. It is the duty of all of us to see that these men get a chance to make good. I thank the chief of the remission branch and the Minister of Justice for the co-operation they have given me. We have got to be very careful in recommending anybody for parole or release on permit. We should thoroughly examine the case in cooperation with the chief of police or the provincial police, and when we are convinced that the boy, man or woman wants to make good and is ready to be released we should trust them and co-operate all the way.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Fort William referred to me twice, and may I say that he and I are not far apart at all. As a matter of fact we are very close. I agree with him completely that the big problem is the man himself and I have never said anything different. When I spoke this afternoon I said not once but at least half a dozen times that in my experience the majority of the law enforcement officers in Canada, including the R.C.M.P., are doing a splendid job in assisting those who have served their penalty. I even said more than that. I said that from my personal knowledge many of them go out of their way to help.
I did say that there was a minority, a few if you like, who did not fall into that class. I drew that to the attention of the minister because, as I explained when I started, in my estimation a forthright statement by the Minister of Justice would mean a great deal to all the law enforcement bodies of Canada. From what the minister said I am certain that he understood me perfectly. The only one who did not understand me, who did not pay attention to what I said about the majority, was the hon. member for Prince Albert. Why he had to pick on my reference to the few is up to him. I think I know the reason why. But what I said was quite clear to the minister. I will give him the information and I am certain, as has been said by the hon. member for Fort William, that the case will

be very carefully investigated in confidence because it involves some persons in the civil service.
While I am on my feet may I say one other thing. Strangely enough, once again I am going to do as I did when I started this afternoon, speak in commendation of the minister and his administration. No matter what party we represent, I believe that if we think the government is wrong we should criticize them as severely as we can, and if we think they are right and are doing a good job we should commend them. I am always prepared to do that and I always have. I have been most interested in an experiment that has been carried on now for approximately two and a half years in the British Columbia penitentiary. As it is an experiment, I presume that the authority for it must have come from the Minister of Justice. I understand it is the only penitentiary in Canada where such an experiment has taken place. It is not costing the government or the taxpayers any money. I am referring to the Dale Carnegie course in the British Columbia penitentiary. It was my privilege to spend two days in the penitentiary as a visitor.
Oh, oh.

I got in and I got out.
Unfortunately the warden was not there on account of ill health, but in the two days I met all the top officials and a great many of the guards and they spoke in the highest terms of this course which was being conducted as an experiment. I spoke to a great number of the inmates, and they were high in their praise of the course. Since that time I have found out that for the last course, which I believe was the third, there were more applicants than the instructor could possibly take because he will not take more than 35.
Since I arrived in Ottawa I have received a number of letters from the inmates who took the first course telling me of the jobs they now hold since they have been released into society, and how this course completely changed their outlook and their attitudes to life. From what I heard from officials of the penitentiary, the guards, the inmates and those who are graduates of the course and who are now back in society, I am convinced that this is perhaps one of the finest experiments ever authorized by the Minister of Justice. It has proven itself in British Columbia. I should like to ask the minister whether he has received reports of this experiment and if so has he made any analysis of them? Is his conclusion that it would be worth while spending the taxpayers
Supply-Justice
money to have the same experiment conducted in all the penitentiaries across Canada? I believe it would be a successful move to rehabilitate those who have broken the law.
Let me say again that I feel this is one of the finest experiments ever conducted. I congratulate the minister upon it. I believe it has proven itself in the one penitentiary to such an extent that it might now be advisable for the department to consider expanding it to include all the penitentiaries in Canada.

Unlike the gentleman who has just taken his seat, it has not been my privilege to spend a day or two in the British Columbia penitentiary, even though it is in my riding. We are not happy about having it in that particular part of the riding, as the Minister of Justice knows, and that is one of the reasons I am rising at this time. I do wish, however, to commend the minister and the mounted police, as well as everyone else who has anything to do with the administration of justice in this country. I think they are doing an excellent job.
I should like to reiterate what the member for Vancouver East said concerning the experiment in the British Columbia institution. In so far as the effect upon the morale of prisoners is concerned, from all the reports I have been receiving I would say that everything the hon. member has said is completely justified. It appears that the experiment is a success.
However, to return to the removal of this particular prison. Many years ago when the district of New Westminster was a small district, it was decided to build a penitentiary along the Fraser river somewhere between what was then known as Sapperton, and the royal city of New Westminster. Since that time the city has grown rapidly, and it has now reached the point where it is almost impossible for anyone to buy property on which to build a home. The penitentiary, because it overlooks the Fraser river, is situated on property with one of the finest views in the whole of British Columbia. The city fathers of New Westminster have indicated from time to time that they wish to have the penitentiary moved. I should like to draw to the minister's attention that if it is possible to have a long-range program in connection with this matter of building penitentiaries certainly one of the first areas to be given consideration should be the New Westminster area. The penitentiary should be moved, let us say, to the Agassiz area, which I understand is desirous of having it, or in some other district that desires it.

Supply-Justice

It has been suggested many times in this house during this session that the minister ought to hold a conference with the attorneys general of the various provinces with respect to the very urgent matter of death on the highways. At this moment I certainly do not propose to deal with that matter. I feel it is a very good suggestion, and the reasons for it have been set forth many times. If such a conference is held by the minister, there is a problem that I think should be on the agenda for consideration, and if such a conference is not held perhaps the minister might consider introducing appropriate legislation to deal with the matter.
The matter with which I wish to deal for a few moments is bicycles and the riders thereof. I am not concerned with adults who ride bicycles. I do not believe that is a matter for proper consideration. Bicycles are here to stay, and adults have to ride them to get to work. It is true that in certain countries, such as England, there are paths on the side of the highway along which adults may ride bicycles. There are certain highways in Ontario, I believe Nos. 400 and 401, upon which bicycles are prohibited. I do not propose to deal with the matter of adults riding bicycles. I am concerned with children who ride bicycles.
I fully realize that the matter of licensing bicycles, and the way they must be lighted, is the concern of the province. I do not wish to touch on that at all. The state is concerned, however, with the welfare of its children. Parents are supposed to be able to look after themselves, but they are also supposed to look after their children. Occasionally we find situations in which parents are not as careful of their children as they might be. In such a case the state has to step in.
Now, the bicycle is a vehicle which arrived before the automobile, and probably for that reason legislation in this respect has not been introduced. I am told, I do not know from personal experience, that 50 years ago there were very few cars on the highway. We had nothing like the traffic situation we have today. Consequently, whether the people who rode bicycles were 50 years of age or ten years of age made little difference. Today, the picture is quite different. Our highways are covered with cars moving at high speeds and with great power. More people own cars in Canada today than ever before. Traffic congestion on our highways, as we all know without going into detail, has become appalling and conditions in the cities are even worse.
Let us compare the bicycle with the automobile for a moment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would indicate whether he is dealing with a matter within the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Justice.

I certainly am, Mr. Chairman. The Department of Justice can pass regulations affecting the person, not the vehicles, and it is to that I am directing my remarks. I am using a bit of background material to illustrate my point. It was recognized at an early date that people had to reach some degree of adult maturity before they were issued licences to drive motor vehicles, inasmuch as they were considered dangerous objects when driven at high speeds, and perhaps by persons without good judgment.
A bicycle is also a vehicle, albeit a human-driven rather than a power-driven vehicle. As I am going to show, a bicycle is just as great a menace when driven by a person without mature judgment as is an automobile. Children ranging from six to nine years who ride on the highways or other widely used public thoroughfares constitute a great menace not only to themselves but to the drivers of automobiles. It is my feeling that the minister should look into the matter as to whether or not children below a certain age-possibly sixteen years or fourteen years -should be prohibited from riding bicycles. I know there would be a great outcry if little Johnnie were to have his bicycle taken away from him, but I do insist that at the present time bicycles ridden by young children constitute a great menace.
I imagine most hon. members drive automobiles and have met with this problem. I do not need to give examples.
