I could say that only last week in my own constituency a horrible accident occurred resulting in the loss of two young lives. Apparently the question as to who was at fault is very much in doubt.
Only the other day when driving to Ottawa from Hull on the narrow interprovincial bridge a small boy who could not have been more than eight or nine years of age, and with an even smaller boy on the handlebars, was weaving in and out of traffic. Finally he fell off, and the smaller one with him. It was only by great good fortune that both of them were not killed instantly.
I do not think I need to say more on the subject, because any automobile driver knows exactly what I mean. In addition to the personal risk involving the loss of life of these young children, there is also the .further fact that indirectly they cause other motor accidents. I am sure many hon. members have had occasion hastily to put on their brakes to avoid hitting a small child on a bicycle weaving in and out of traffic, or passing on

the wrong side. Sometimes these young children ride down the street three or four abreast. They cannot help being a menace to traffic, and also to themselves.
The statistical material-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I dislike very much raising a point of order, but I really believe the subject matter which my hon. friend is discussing is clearly not our concern here, unless his proposal would be that we should make it a crime for certain persons to ride a bicycle. Since we have the power to pass laws making certain acts crimes that is the way we would have to do it. However, I believe most provinces have municipal acts under which the municipalities are empowered to pass bylaws regulating the riding of bicycles. And it is much better that they should pass such laws, because there would be many municipalities in which bicycle traffic would represent no hazard at all, while in others it would represent a great hazard. Each municipality should have the law which best suits its needs. With all deference to my hon. friend, I do not think it is a matter which comes under our jurisdiction here.

I quite agree with the minister, that there are other considerations of which account must be taken. But I do point out that legislation could be introduced by the minister which would make it a criminal offence for a person of, let us say, under fourteen or sixteen years of age to ride a bicycle, f am only advocating that the minister examine the subject thoroughly.
He has just brought up the interesting point that in the backwoods areas, where there might be little traffic, there is no menace presented either to the child riding the bicycle or to automobile drivers, but that the situation is quite different in the more heavily populated areas. I am bringing up the point so that it can be considered, as I thought I had made clear at the beginning of my remarks.
If the minister has no objection I shall take only a moment to conclude what I have to say, by placing on record certain statistical information which, I might add, is not of much help to us.
Why give it, then?

The statistical information is not of much help to us, and if a conference is held I would hope that the minister would try to obtain further information. I feel this is a very important subject.
Figures from the Canada Year Book indicate that in 1950 there were 55 persons killed while riding bicycles in Canada-and these figures are exclusive of Quebec. There appear
Supply-J ustice
to be no traffic figures available for that province. In 1951 there were 55 killed, and in 1952 there were 52. However, the figures for injuries are somewhat different. In 1950 there were 1,656 persons injured while riding bicycles in this country-again, exclusive of Quebec. In 1951 there were 1,673 and in 1952 there were 1,874, showing a steady increase.
There has been no breaking down of these figures into age groups and, as I said before, the figures do not include Quebec.
As I suggested earlier, perhaps the minister might look into the problem and discuss it with the attorneys general of the provinces. It would be a step toward the saving of young lives, would prevent injury and also prevent the snarling of traffic on our increasingly crowded highways and thoroughfares.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Kootenay West.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman; I have been most patient. I had intended to talk on this item for two or three minutes about the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but inasmuch as that subject has been discussed by several speakers, I shall make my remarks brief.
I might tell the minister that as a boy I had a very dim view of the Royal North West Mounted Police, as it was then known. I was in the woods fighting with a boy friend of mine, when a man who claimed to be a member of that force came along, arrested me and locked me up in the small wooden jail, in a room about 10 by 16. I was let out that evening and was thoroughly indignant, as you can understand.
A friend of ours owned a beautiful ranch, and lived within 10 miles of us. He had gone to Nelson for some time. This same self-styled police officer took another English settler out to that ranch, sold it to him, obtained his down payment and then left the district. Shortly thereafter we found he was not a member of the Royal North West Mounted Police, and naturally our opinion of the police force changed.
I listened with keen interest to what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I am sure those cases must be very few and far between. I know the minister will investigate thoroughly and give the results of the investigation to the house. I must say my experience for a good many years has been one of increased respect for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I have found them to be officers and men showing courtesy and tact. Since I was a boy I have known a number of inspectors, officers and members of the force. I served overseas with

Supply-Justice
some of them, and have always been very much impressed by their impartiality and the high grade of their work. In my opinion their efficiency, courtesy and fairness has been demonstrated in my district on several occasions.
A most difficult situation arose in connection with the transportation of the Japanese to the interior. Most of them came to the Kootenays. The matter was handled efficiently and with courtesy. Every consideration was given to human feelings, and every sympathy was shown for these unfortunate people who were moved into that district at that time. Then, during the policing of those camps, there was nothing but general commendation of the attitude of the officers and men in charge of that work. The most interesting illustration is the occasions when the R.C.M.P. have been called in to deal with the Sons of Freedom. I think that is a test of discipline, of efficiency, of tact and of great forbearance under extreme provocation. When you come to handle anywhere from 100 to 300 or 400 naked Sons of Freedom you have an unusual problem from a police point of view, and a problem which puts the police under such circumstances under great provocation. I have personal knowledge, Mr. Chairman, of the very efficient and humane way in which the R.C.MP. handled several very difficult and tantalizing situations.
Previous to the remarks of the speakers concerning the R.C.M.P. I had intended to rise principally to point out also that their fairness, their impartiality and their knowledge of their responsibility to the people of Canada as a whole was well demonstrated on April 28 of this year when two R.C.M.P. constables stopped General Foulkes in a car, in which was sitting the Minister of National Defence, because the car failed to have the necessary licence plates. I have heard appreciation of that action expressed by a number of people whom I have met since then and during the last week, as I have just returned from opening one of the most important airports in Canada. This action on the part of the two R.C.M.P. constables indicates very clearly to the Canadian people that neither rank, prestige nor position is a defence against the law. I think it also indicates very clearly that the civil power in this country, those forces that are given the duty to administer the law, are still supreme, and I would suggest to the minister, as it has been suggested to me by persons who have discussed the matter with me, that those two constables deserve commendation from their senior officers for their impartial attitude in such circumstances.

Just before this item passes I should like to ask the minister two or three questions. Perhaps I could wait until the particular item comes up, but then I am always up against the proposition that I should have asked it before. Some weeks ago an item appeared in the London Free Press dealing with thievery at Camp Ipperwash. The item in the Free Press went on to state that civilians were stopped on the street of a town near Camp Ipperwash and that allegedly stolen goods were taken from those civilians right on the street. That seemed to me to be a rather unusual procedure. Since that time there has been a rather ominous silence as far as the newspapers are concerned. I have not heard anything more about it. Under what statute did the R.C.M.P. act in a case like that? What report, if any, has the minister regarding this alleged offence at Camp Ipperwash and the apprehension of civilians in those towns adjacent to the area? What action, if any, has been taken against the wrongdoers? Have any charges been laid? What happened in the matter? Personally, as far as I am concerned, from any experience that I have had with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, their work has been efficiently done, and I am just bringing this up because of the interest many of my constituents have in the articles that appeared in the newspaper at that time.

I could not tell the minister but I will find it out for him.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the various words of criticism and praise that have been applied to the R.C.M.P. and I am not going to make any extended remarks along that line.
I have a very high regard for the R.C.M.P. Those members of the force whom I have known and with whom I have had anything to do have been gentlemen and have attempted to do a real good job. I believe the historic tradition of the R.C.M.P. still lives on.
Of course, we have got to recognize that there is a difference in the constitutional make-up of all men and that includes policemen. You find some who are pretty abrupt and have perhaps the police complex, but you find others who are very courteous and chummy.
I recall on one occasion I was driving at night and suddenly in front of me I saw a flashlight going on and I thought I had better stop in case there had been an accident. I stopped and it was not long before an R.CM.P. constable came up to my window. I pulled the glass down and he more or less bellowed into my ear, "Where is your driver's licence?" I was a little taken aback, but I held my composure a bit and I said, "Why, it is in my pocket." He said, "Let me see it," and I said, "Well, I will if you say 'please'." And that took him aback a little bit and I had a little more time in which to recompose myself. I said to him, "I will tell you what I will do. I will let you see my card and I will be pleased to show you my driver's licence if you ask nicely for it." I added, "There is such a thing as common courtesy."

I gave him my card with my name on it and he walked around my car and came back again and he was writing something down. I fancied he was writing down the licence number, and I put my car into low gear and began driving slowly away. Then I put it in second gear and it was not long until I was away. He never saw my driver's licence. I rather expected that I might receive a subpoena to appear in police court the next day, but I never received one. I just say that I do not think that is particularly characteristic of our R.C.M.P. However, there is a difference in their make-up. We cannot expect them to be smiling at all times although, when they have a little job to do, it is nice if they are pleasant. Mr. Chairman, I did not rise necessarily for the purpose of saying that, although I want to go on record as saying and believing that the R.C.M.P. for the most part are an extremely commendable force.
I rose particularly, Mr. Chairman, to bring to the attention of the minister something that I know he must be greatly concerned about. The background of what I have to say originates in the case of a young man who, not so long ago, committed a murder, was sent up for trial and was sentenced to be hanged. He was a young man just 18 years of age. Fortunately-I fancy fortunately; in some people's view, fortunately-the remission branch commuted his sentence to life imprisonment. The whole case caused a tremendous stir throughout this nation, particularly in the community in which the crime was committed and the trial was held. Much publicity was given to the case by press and radio, and I followed it with a good deal of interest. It seemed to me that the whole case was one involving what today we commonly term the problem of juvenile delinquency. I know that the minister has a tremendous job on his hands, but this matter is becoming a serious problem not only to this nation but also to other nations. I refer to this sort of hoodlum gang of teen-agers who seem to roam our streets and thrive on wickedness. I assert that they are no good to anyone and that they are really a blot on our society. The case I mentioned gave rise to a good deal of comment and a good deal of extremely sound editorial comment. I want to congratulate the press on their editorial comments. They brought out some fine suggestions and observations not merely with respect to the case itself but with respect to the whole matter of juvenile delinquency.
I have been greatly interested in this subject for a good many years because I have had some little experience in directing and running boys' summer camps; and I have taken a course or two in the study of youth 83276-347
Supply-Justice
and related subjects of that kind. I used to hold that there never was such a thing as a bad boy. But sometimes, in my problems, my mind would wander and I would begin to take a different position altogether and to conclude that there never was such a thing as a good boy. Be that as it may, Mr. Chairman, the basic problem of juvenile delinquency is there. We can talk all we like about punishment and about the punitive angle in relation to our criminal law and yet ignore the influences leading up to the crime that juvenile delinquency can be charged with.
There must be some basic reason for the problem. I know that the minister is just as greatly concerned about the problem as is anyone else. After all, he is responsible for the administration of justice throughout the country. Basically, I think the problem can be stated in this way. There is a disregard for the eternal concept which has been true throughout human history-the concept, in fact, that cannot be escaped-namely that a man is a responsible being, responsible to his fellow man and to his Creator and Judge. I have no use for this mollycoddling of young people whenever they do that which is wrong.
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver East stated this afternoon that he was glad to see that we were coming to a time when we were doing away with the punitive angle of our whole concept of administering justice in respect of crime. I do not know that I altogether agree with him in that particular statement. At least I am not glad. We may be getting away from the punitive principle in relation to crime. However, he did not state that at the same time crime was on the increase. I agree with him in a good deal that he said. I agree that in the rehabilitation of criminals there must be something more than simply punishment. However, I am still just old-fashioned enough to believe what Solomon said about sparing the rod and spoiling the child. Yet I am a family man and am extremely proud of my family and of the way they have turned out. However, that is neither here nor there.
I know the problem must give the minister some concern because we read in the papers not long ago what was said by a commissioner appointed, I believe, by the Quebec government. I think that is so, although the newspaper report does not say so. I will read it to the minister. It is headed "Too Many Youth in Penitentiaries" and reads as follows:
Too many Canadian teen-agers are feeing sent to prison, the federal penitentiaries commissioner says in his report for the year ended March 31 last.
Commissioner R. B. Gibson said in his report to parliament-
I fancy he means to the legislature.

Supply-J ustice
Parliament.

Perhaps the minister will correct me there. The article continues: -that, of the total penitentiary population on March 31, 564, or 11-4 per cent were under 21 years of age.
One boy of 13 was doing a term,-
That evidently is the one referred to a little while ago.
-seventeen others were under 16 and forty-eight were 16. Major General Gibson lamented the fact that so many Quebec youngsters were being sent to jail. "The continuing committal of youths of 14 to 18 is a matter of grave concern. Too many youths are being sent to the penitentiaries for lack of an adequate number of provincially operated reformatory institutions. Probation is not being used to the extent possible as an alternative to incarceration."
I read that because I know the minister must be concerned with the situation, but nevertheless I still maintain that the more important thing is that there must be influences leading up to the point where there is such a thing as juvenile delinquency. I know the minister's problem is one of administration of the law after crimes have been committed, and I am talking about something else for which I can hardly make him responsible.
The reason I rise on this occasion is to put forth something that is of tremendous interest to me, and I am just wondering if he has considered whether his administration can be correlated with other organizations throughout the country, municipal, provincial and so on, that are doing their best to obviate juvenile delinquency. What I have in mind is this. We have often heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare say that his department is very much concerned with preventive medicine. That is good. We often ask him what he is doing in connection with the health of the nation and he says that he is interested in preventive medicine. I think we should ask the Minister of Justice to what extent his department might be able to exercise influence in preventing crimes rather than spending so much time and energy in administering the law after crimes have been committed.
There are several matters that I think I might refer to under this head. Not so long ago Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, who is Britain's home secretary and is charged with enforcing the law and bringing criminals to justice, made a speech in which he gave a number of reasons for the phenomenal increase in crime during the last decade. He had this to say:
There used to be a feeling in regard to the ordinary unimportant aspects of life that when one did wrong it was an offence to God as well as an unpleasant thing to do. It is vitally important that there should be the recognition that crime is

wrong in the moral sense and that punishment is deserved. This view is often absent from the minds of those who come before the courts.
The problem which most impresses me is this: Can we, in the second half of this lunatic twentieth century into which we have been born, make the spiritual stature of man at least approximately commensurate with the scientific advances for which he is responsible? If we can, the hopes of changing a mad century into a sane one are enormous.
The same gentleman, Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, said that there were perhaps four things that are responsible for juvenile delinquency in particular, and I know that the minister cannot control them. He said that the first one is the lack of parental control. I am afraid that he put his finger on a vital spot. I believe our parents have got to indicate to their children that when they do wrong punishment is sure. Personally I have no use for all this talk which I label a sort of quack psychology. The second cause to which he referred is the increasing problem of broken homes which contributes to juvenile delinquency. The report the minister read concerning the 13-year-old boy indicated that he has the background of a broken home. The third point, said Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, is that false values are propagated by motion pictures and the modern pulp literature. I want to dwell on that for a moment because here is where I believe the Minister of Justice and his department can be of some help.
I know they claim to have no jurisdiction over the censorship of motion pictures, but there is no question in my mind that motion pictures as they are shown on the screen today have a tremendous effect upon our juveniles. Television is now beginning to come into its own in Canada and if it is permitted to go to the same lengths in what it portrays I rather despair of the juveniles of the coming generation. If I had my way, Mr. Chairman, I would not permit a hold-up scene to be shown in a motion picture theatre. If I had my way I would not permit guns to be fired in any scene shown in a motion picture theatre. I would not permit murder to be shown. Neither would I permit a drinking scene. Some people may scorn that view-
But you are right just the same.

-but the proof of the pudding is in what is happening. That is the proof. The modern motion picture is largely responsible for what youngsters learn about these things. When people are grown up and are mature, sensible and stable the situation may be a little different. Certain motion pictures are advertised as adult entertainment and some of the teen-agers

say: This is going to be juicy, we will go to see it. These are things that have to be faced, and I say that we must tackle this problem from the standpoint of the influences that lead up to the commission of crime.
We do not have to go very far from this building to see the results of the hoodlum gang. Go to some of the restaurants and drop in for a pot of tea at the time when young people are leaving the dance halls and the "pubs". I have done that. I like a pot of tea before going to bed, and I can tell you that on one or two occasions I actually have been frightened enough to leave the restaurant. On looking around outside I was not able to see a policeman anywhere. Perhaps they know what is happening and they are around the corner somewhere out of sight. You do not have to go far to see the results of what I call the hoodlum gang.
There is another cause responsible for juvenile delinquency, the lessening of the power of religion-
Hear, hear.

-in the ordinary affairs of life. I do not say this because of my profession. I think it is common sense that if any boy-or girl-is brought up to believe that he is responsible to his fellow men and to his Creator, and that crime is punishable, and is taught to respect the great moral principles of life, he will have before him the greatest deterrent to crime that could be devised. However, I am afraid that is seriously lacking.
I am not going to talk tonight as though I were talking to a conference of preachers, because I know I am not. Believe me, if I were talking to a conference of preachers on this subject, I would give them hell.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Order.

I am rather hard on preachers. I believe they have a real job to do. There are too many soft soapers instead of facing right up to the real facts of life. There is too much mollycoddling of that which is wrong, and countenancing of that which is wrong by saying they do not mean any harm. Let us not kid ourselves.
Now, Mr. Chairman, those are some of the things which I believe are lacking in our social life today. I come now to the main point. I should like to ask what the government can do about it. Well, I think they could do a lot about it. I do not know that I want to focus the responsibility for this on the Minister of Justice. Perhaps he will say that is someone else's department. I believe that this government should bring 83276-347J

into existence throughout this country great recreational institutions, parks, and so on. They could be put into operation with trained young people as leaders, men and women who are expert along that line. It is done in a very small and modified way by some municipalities, but I believe it could be done to a greater extent. There is need for youth leaders to go out and create in young people today a real regard for the moral principles of life.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member will agree with me that perhaps I am entitled at this time to ask him if he will please get back into the Department of Justice.

Mr. Chairman, I fully agree with you, but I do not agree with those who applauded you. There is one other point I should like to mention. I do not know whether or not it is possible for the Department of Justice to introduce any particular law of this kind. They may say that it is outside their jurisdiction altogether. I am a great believer in the curfew. I am a great believer that young people should be home at a proper time. I am a great believer that the place of young people at night is in the home. Some of our smaller municipalities have the curfew, and I think it works well. I do not know whether the Minister of Justice agrees with that, but I should like to have some expression from him as to whether his department has seriously considered some method whereby they could synchronize their work with the various organizations throughout the country to curb, so far as possible, this thing which is becoming, as we must recognize, a menace to our social life and to our country; this thing we call juvenile delinquency. I feel the minister should answer that question and tell the committee just what he thinks can be done.

I am sure many members of this house sitting here tonight must have been shocked, as I was, to hear some of the words which have just been spoken. I think it is a great pity that the vast majority of devoted and earnest clergymen in this country should have been maligned by an ex-colleague, whose associations have apparently been most unfortunate.

163. Remission service, including $10,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by treasury board, $137,276.

I notice there is provision in this item for $10,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies. Tonight I have been

Supply-J ustice
listening with interest, in some cases, to a discussion of the situation prevailing within prisons and penitentiaries. Many tributes have been made to the improvements that have taken place in these institutions since the end of the war. I would agree heartily with those statements. It has been rather interesting to hear the several members confess their respective criminal records so far as contact with prison institutions is concerned; that is all to the good, I am sure, because open confession is good for the soul.
I, too, have some confession to make. I belong to the pre-Archambault report group of folk who were associated with prisons and penitentiaries in this country. I know that there is now a vast difference in the internal atmosphere as compared to the years 1938, 1939 and 1940, when I went in and out of several penal institutions in this country. I do not want to emphasize that particular aspect of the problem; that progress is excellent. I should like to say, however, that good institutional care is of little value unless some attention is given to the matter of after-care, the very crucial period in the experience of a prisoner when he is trying to re-establish contact with the community.
You can house him in a palace, you can subject him to all the remedial programs that there are in the book of modern penology, but unless something is done to soften the shock of readjustment to the outside world then there is great possibility that the improvement in conditions in the institutions will be wasted. We are all aware that particularly servicemen, who spent four or five years in some branch of the armed forces, had to pass through a rehabilitation program. Life in the services was so unique, cutting them off from regular society, that considerable sums of money were spent in helping the servicemen to readjust themselves to society.
I think the same problem faces the prisoner who has spent a period of time in one of the penal institutions. First of all, he becomes somewhat of an institutionalized personality who has been subjected to a more or less rigorous routine, and who has been suddenly projected into the outside world to fend for himself, and who often finds such adjustment very difficult indeed.
From my three years' active work in this field I found that the real problem of the prisoner begins after discharge. He is not too badly off when he is under institutional care. But upon release he faces for the first time the social stigma of being branded as someone who has served time. This confronts him first of all in hunting for a job. A good many prisoners find it almost impossible to

re-establish themselves in civilian occupations, because as soon as their prison records become known to prospective employers, their chances of obtaining work are gone. I would point out that because of this stigma which attaches to penal servitude, even the Canadian civil service will not employ a discharged prisoner. I know that on many occasions we could not find' employment for discharged prisoners in ordinary positions. This was in the early days of the war. We arranged a scheme whereby we contacted farmers out west who would accept responsibility for one of these discharged prisoners until such time as he could fend for himself in the labour market. In most cases the only chance of securing employment was where it was possible for the agency working in the field of prisoner rehabilitation to make contact with a sympathetic employer who understood the circumstances and was willing to co-operate in helping a prisoner make a successful readjustment to society.
There has been much comment this evening on the efficiency of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is one of the finest police forces in the world; but I discovered that, although the situation is improving, sometimes municipal police were not too much in sympathy with the after-care problem of the discharged prisoner. If a crime occurred in a local area the municipal police would proceed immediately to investigate thoroughly any of the men in that area who had prison records, and would not be too careful in their approach to the matter. They would approach an employer and reveal that a particular employee had a criminal record, with the result that the employee again found himself foot-loose and fancy free.
This reference to recognized prisoners' aid societies provides an opportunity to discuss this very important problem. There has been some comment to the effect that in Canada we do not use the parole system as widely as possible. Certainly we do not use it to as great an extent as one finds in the United States or even in the United Kingdom. The experience in those countries has shown that wherever possible it is desirable to get prisoners out from under institutional care as quickly as possible, so that they may make a successful readjustment in their communities. Certainly there is no merit in prolonging the period of imprisonment within an institution. Today, when the emphasis is on the remedial rather than on the punitive aspect in the treatment of criminals, the desire is to get the criminal back into society so that he may fill a useful place in the community with his fellow citizens.

There are three private agencies operating in the field of prisoner after-care. They are the John Howard Society, the Elizabeth Fry Society, and the Salvation Army. I would be interested to know just how far the federal government goes in supporting the excellent work of these private agencies in this very important field. I repeat that the best institutions in the land, equipped with all modern techniques, psychiatrists, psychologists, work programs, and all the other aids, are of little avail unless we can overcome the problem that arises when the discharged prisoner comes in contact with society. It is not his performance in the prison institution with which we are concerned; it is his performance as a free citizen in the broader community.
Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to answer my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not sure whether I have properly comprehended the main point of my hon. friend's question, but I hope he will correct me if I have not done so. I understood him to be asking what we can do to prevent juvenile delinquency.
To synchronize the work of your department with that of other organizations in Canada which are attempting to prevent juvenile delinquency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as the rehabilitation of prisoners is concerned, we can do and we have been doing a great deal. When the prisoners enter a penitentiary they come in contact at once with a classification officer who is a trained psychologist and who, in relation to each one of them, makes out a card index record. He discusses with them their previous history, their family background and aptitudes. He prepares a study of their cases in the same way that a personnel officer does in a large and efficient industry. He keeps in periodical contact with each prisoner during his whole term in prison, and advises him as to the vocational training course he should take. He advises him as to the way in which he can rehabilitate himself after his discharge. He makes contacts with organizations such as the John Howard Society and the Salvation Army, which will provide the after-care about which the hon. member for Brandon spoke. In that way he assists the discharged prisoner to make a successful rehabilitation as an honest man in civilian life.
Our record is a very good one in the matter of the rehabilitation of prisoners who have been in our penitentiaries. The rate of recidivism from our institutions is very much lower than it is from any of the other institutions in Canada, and is improving all the time. But if
Supply-Justice
my hon. friend is speaking about the prevention of juvenile delinquency and crime, the prevention of the coming of prisoners into the penitentiary in the first place, then I think he is dealing with a subject matter which, in almost all of its aspects, is the responsibility of the provinces. Take the matter of the curfew. We have no authority over that, likewise we have no authority over the censoring of the movies; we have no authority over the enforcement of the laws that we pass here with regard to crime comics or obscene literature. It was contemplated when our country was created that the federal government would have all those functions which deal with national matters-defence, banking and commerce and the money supply, the interest rate, interprovincial railway and highway traffic, interprovincial commerce, international affairs and the like. On the other hand all of those matters which related to the individual as a person, education, property and civil rights, and that sort of thing, all local institutions and controls come under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments and legislatures.
The only way in which we can assist in the prevention of crime where it originates in the local communities is by helping the provinces discharge their responsibilities by means of dominion-provincial tax agreements and other like arrangements. By these means we have tried to put every province in Canada in a position to provide a reasonable minimum service under all of those heads, if they wish to do so; but we have no direct contact with or direct responsibility for most of the influences that would have to do with the prevention of crime.
Ten o'clock.

I do not want to hold up the item, but I want to say a word with relation to the staff of the remission service. In our association with the special committee on capital and corporal punishment, some of us, myself included, have come to realize-others may have already done so-the difficulties of the very important and hard-working branch of the department. I just want to say that I know the minister's difficulties in connection with the staff, particularly the senior staff of that branch. I should like to hear from him what steps are being taken to ensure that this branch and his department generally will be adequately staffed. I know he has difficulties in that regard which we can perhaps help him to overcome. I know the minister's department is rather short of staff at the moment.
